_Why does an agent that can search everything it has ever stored still act on the wrong facts?_

A context window holds the working state of one model call, and retained attention state only accelerates computation over that same prefix. Neither decides what an agent should still know across sessions, system restarts, or extended operational horizons. Providing an agent with persistent memory requires an external storage architecture that can index heterogeneous experiences, retrieve relevant historical context without polluting active prompts, and resolve conflicting observations over time. However, semantic vector retrieval alone provides no temporal guarantees. Stale facts, superseded code versions, and contradicted preferences score just as highly in cosine similarity as fresh ground truth. The runtime must therefore treat every stored memory as a fallible claim that carries its provenance, the versions for which it holds, and an explicit path to invalidation. Reliability depends on keeping persistent state behind explicit consistency rules rather than trusting the model to reconcile contradictory historical evidence.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Classify persistent records by their source, evidential role, and relationship to derived search representations
- Specify a retrieval contract that bounds access, returned content, resource use, and required freshness
- Choose among pre-staged evidence, a direct read, and model-directed search from how much of the need the task names
- Select retrieval methods for an information need, use a bandwidth floor to screen exact vector scans against a latency budget, and estimate multi-hop evidence against a serialized-token budget
- Design a memory write policy for admission, correction, supersession, expiry, and deletion that keeps derived summaries from perpetuating a withdrawn claim
- Explain version-aware exclusion and fallback without mistaking removal of stale candidates for complete fresh retrieval
- Evaluate cross-session memory policies by task outcomes, update behavior, and total resource cost

:::

## Memory Beyond One Session {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-introduction}

Consider the repair agent (lighthouse \ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}) working on its connection-pool defect across several sessions. When the initial session terminates, the subsequent run must reconstruct the operational state: the candidate source tree at revision `r18`, the diagnostic failure observed at `r17`, the passing run of `test_waiter_notified_on_return`, the integration checks that remain unresolved, and an operational note indicating where to resume execution. None of this state survives inside a transient context window once the process exits. Persisting only the final summary message discards critical supporting evidence. Conversely, retaining raw message transcripts without explicit scope creates confusion; an agent reading an unannotated log can easily mistake an earlier failure under `r17` for an error in the new candidate patch.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_s.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with the State axis highlighted."}

*Durable State, closed by checking each retrieved record against its source.*
:::

Standard runtime mechanisms do not bridge this gap. Context engineering selects among information already staged for a single model call, while the inference serving system maintains key-value (KV) attention cache state purely to accelerate that computation. Although a prefix cache can outlive an individual request, it remains a derived acceleration structure for a compatible prompt prefix (principle \ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}), regardless of the storage medium holding it. Long-term memory addresses a different systems problem, preserving information that must govern decisions across distinct invocations. A durable memory system must explicitly resolve what records to retain, how to index and retrieve them efficiently, and how to update or invalidate them when external sources change. In the formal framing of @sec-vol3-intro-hsa, these records constitute durable State ($\StateExposureLevel_3$), persisting across session boundaries.

Architecting persistent memory for an agent requires solving three interconnected systems problems. First, the data model must establish explicit record roles that keep external sources, tool observations, and agent-authored notes strictly differentiated, ensuring that subsequent sessions recognize what evidence each record supports. Second, the system requires a retrieval contract. Regardless of the candidate generation mechanism, every read must report its query scope, the snapshot versions it admitted, and whether the search terminated cleanly or degraded under resource budgets. Third, the storage engine needs a write lifecycle that admits, updates, supersedes, expires, and deletes records while propagating those mutations to downstream indexes and summaries.

The chapter takes these problems in the order a read depends on them. Record roles come first (@sec-vol3-persistent-need), because every later indexing, retrieval, and invalidation policy depends on knowing what authority a stored record carries. The retrieval contract (@sec-vol3-persistent-governance) then fixes what any read must specify and report, whatever index sits behind it, and the choice between pre-staged and model-directed retrieval (@sec-vol3-long-term-memory-agentic-retrieval) decides which component formulates the query. Three method sections match index structures to information needs, moving from names and syntax (@sec-vol3-persistent-bm25) through learned representations and fused rankings (@sec-vol3-persistent-dense-retrieval) to chains of related evidence (@sec-vol3-persistent-graphrag). The write path (@sec-vol3-long-term-memory-write-path) and storage invalidation (@sec-vol3-persistent-invalidation) keep the store and its derived indexes truthful as sources change, and the final section (@sec-vol3-persistent-governance-eval) judges a complete memory policy by the tasks it helps finish across sessions.

## Persistent Records {#sec-vol3-persistent-need}

When an autonomous agent repairs a system across multiple sessions, it relies on records that serve different operational purposes. The repository source defines what the code looks like at a given commit; an execution log records how a test behaved under specific runtime parameters; a progress note guides the subsequent session on where to resume work. Systems designers must distinguish these roles explicitly. Retrieval strategies, cache validation, and deletion policies all depend on the operational function of the record in question.

### Record roles {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-record-roles}

Most persistent state an agent consumes originates outside its execution loop, in version-controlled repositories, production databases, system configurations, and user profiles. Other records arise during execution, including raw environment observations, tool output traces, synthesized progress summaries, and speculative heuristics. Treating these diverse artifacts as undifferentiated "agent memory" obscures the critical distinction between a verifiable ground truth and a derived claim. @Tbl-vol3-memory-tiers categorizes these records by their architectural role in the evidence chain.

| **Record role**          | **Example**                                                                                    | **What a later use must preserve**                                                        |
|:-------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Source record            | `src/pool.py` at a specified revision; the user's stated scheduling preference                 | The designated source, applicable version or scope, and access conditions                 |
| Observation or event log | The outcome of `test_waiter_notified_on_return` under recorded source, test, and configuration | What was observed, when, and under which conditions; gaps in the retained history         |
| Agent-written memory     | A progress note, session summary, or proposed repair lesson                                    | Supporting records, uncertainty, intended scope, and the policy for correction or removal |
| Derived retrieval index  | Search entries over source files, logs, or notes                                               | Which source generation produced the entry and how changes affect its use                 |

: **Roles of persistent records**: These are roles in an evidence chain, not a hierarchy of storage devices or universal levels of trust. One record can serve more than one role. {#tbl-vol3-memory-tiers tbl-colwidths="[23,33,44]"}

A **source of record**\index{Source of record!definition} is the designated authoritative origin for a specific claim. For example, the Git tree serves as the source of record for a file's contents at a particular commit hash, while an authenticated user message serves as the source of record for that user's operational constraints. Establishing a source of record defines where any downstream assertion must be validated. It confers evidential provenance rather than correctness. A repository commit may harbor a regression, and an inline code comment may contain unauthorized instructions. Under the principle that authority stays with the source (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority})\index{Principle!authority stays with the source}, authority describes an evidentiary relationship between a claim and its origin, never an unconstrained permission grant. When an agent's generated output drifts from its source of record, the output still binds whoever deployed the agent, as one tribunal made explicit in the case that follows. For a memory system, the further question is what happens when such an answer is kept and read again.

::: {#ws-06-moffatt-air-canada-2024 .callout-war-story title="A support chatbot contradicts its policy page (2024)"}

**Context**: In November 2022, following the death of his grandmother, passenger Jake Moffatt consulted the customer-support chatbot on Air Canada's website regarding bereavement fares [@moffatt2024aircanada]. Air Canada's formal bereavement policy, published on a separate page of the website, explicitly prohibited retroactive bereavement fare adjustments once travel was completed.

**Mechanism**: The chatbot erroneously informed Moffatt that he could purchase regular-fare tickets immediately and submit a bereavement refund claim within 90 days of ticket issuance, directly contradicting the airline's published policy. When Moffatt submitted his claim, Air Canada denied it based on the static policy page. Before the British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal, Air Canada argued that the chatbot was an independent legal entity responsible for its own actions.

**Impact**: The tribunal rejected Air Canada's argument, finding that the chatbot was an integral component of Air Canada's website and that the airline remained liable for all information published through it. Finding Air Canada liable for negligent misrepresentation, the tribunal ordered the airline to pay CA\$650.88 in damages (representing the difference between the full fare and the bereavement rate), alongside interest and statutory tribunal fees.

**Fix**: The tribunal dismissed the assertion that customers must independently reconcile conflicting guidance across different website pages, holding that deployers bear full responsibility for auditing and aligning interactive automated assistants with published corporate policies.

**Systems lesson**: A generated response is a derived artifact, yet users and legal frameworks treat it as an authoritative corporate commitment. The engineering remedy is to stage the versioned source of record into the model call and constrain the answer to claims that text supports, which is the job of the retrieval contract developed below. Model fluency provides neither evidentiary validity nor legal protection.

:::

Through the taxonomy of @tbl-vol3-memory-tiers, the published policy page functioned as the source of record, while the chatbot's generated response was a derived artifact that diverged from ground truth. If a customer-support system logs its previous dialogue turns to inform future responses, those conversational turns become agent-written memory. They document past interactions, but they never constitute organizational policy. A store that kept the chatbot's wrong answer and retrieved it for the next bereavement question would repeat the error with the apparent weight of precedent, unless the record carried its role as a derived answer and a link to the policy version it claimed to reflect.

Observation logs capture empirical execution history. When an agent tests a connection pool, an execution log showing a failure at revision `r17` remains invaluable diagnostic history even after revision `r18` resolves the bug. The subsequent passing run confirms that the specific reproducer succeeded under that exact environment configuration. An execution log provides primary evidence of what the system observed during a run, rather than proving the universal validity of any underlying program assertion. Retaining this historical record across machine restarts or worker failures requires durable persistence guarantees.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Durable, replicated logs that survive worker and machine failures are developed in @sec-vol3-persistence-event-sourcing.
:::

Agent-written memory synthesizes raw observations into structured artifacts for future execution steps, taking the form of scratchpad notes, session summaries, or learned heuristics. Condensing raw traces prevents repetitive computation and conserves context window capacity. However, summarization introduces its own failure modes, because compression can strip vital boundary conditions or fabricate causal explanations. For instance, the observation that the targeted reproducer passed at `r18` is strictly justified by the execution log. In contrast, the generalized claim that connection-pool timeouts always stem from missed thread notifications asserts a universal rule that a single test execution cannot substantiate. Storing an unsupported generalization in a persistent database creates compounding errors in subsequent planning steps.

This divergence mirrors the foundational distinction from cognitive psychology [@tulving1972episodic] adopted by agent architectures: **episodic memory**\index{Episodic memory!definition} captures discrete, time-stamped events anchored to specific execution contexts, whereas **semantic memory**\index{Semantic memory!definition} stores generalized knowledge, rules, and abstractions extracted across multiple episodes, complemented by **procedural memory**\index{Procedural memory!definition} that preserves executable workflows, tool scripts, and operational runbooks. In the terms of @tbl-vol3-memory-tiers, observation logs and episode summaries are episodic records, generated lessons and reference facts are semantic records, and reusable repair workflows represent procedural records. In an engineered system, semantic and procedural records are therefore derived artifacts whose epistemic validity depends entirely on the fidelity and scope of the underlying episodic records.

A retrieval index serves as an auxiliary acceleration structure for locating information across storage tiers. Whether an index stores term postings, learned vector embeddings, or graph edges over source files, logs, and agent notes (structures this chapter develops in turn), indexing only facilitates discovery. When a search query matches an index entry, a high similarity score demonstrates lexical or semantic affinity to the query string, but provides no assurance of operational applicability to the current task. Operational applicability depends on whether the referenced record matches the current system state, schema revision, and environment constraints.

### Read and write lifecycle {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-read-write-lifecycle}

Consider the state of a code-repair agent immediately after it writes revision `r18`. If its vector or keyword index was generated from revision `r17`, a retrieval query for `src/pool.py` will return the unpatched file. While that record remains an accurate historical reflection of `r17`, serving it as current context leads the model to believe the bug persists, prompting redundant or conflicting edits. The staleness that context invalidation guards against thus extends beyond the active prompt into the persistent storage tiers that feed subsequent inference calls.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Context invalidation, which withdraws a staged observation's authority over current state once its source changes, is established in @sec-vol3-context-engineering-context-rot.
:::

Precomputing search indexes eliminates the need to scan large repositories or execution histories during inference. However, this optimization incurs an ongoing synchronization cost. Every update to a source file requires indexing new content and invalidating or evicting obsolete embeddings. Executing these updates synchronously blocks read or write operations, while background asynchronous indexing opens a lag window in which the index still answers from `r17` although the file is already at `r18`. A query that arrives inside that window needs an explicit rule for what it may return, which @sec-vol3-long-term-memory-index-coordination supplies.

Conversational agents meet the same consistency problem in user state. A user who said "Schedule no meetings before 10:00 AM" later says "before 11:00 AM." The two directives are nearly identical as text, yet their intent is mutually exclusive. A store that treats the second as a duplicate keeps the stale behavior, and one that appends it without retiring the first leaves a contradiction in every later prompt. Telling a complementary fact from a superseding one requires explicit lifecycle metadata, which the write path (@sec-vol3-long-term-memory-write-path) supplies and carries to every derived index, alongside validation, time-to-live (TTL) expiration, and cascade deletion.

The read side comes first, because lifecycle metadata protects the agent only if every read reports it. A retrieval interface must therefore return candidate text alongside the provenance, version, and completeness information on which safe execution depends.

## The Retrieval Contract {#sec-vol3-persistent-governance}

Diagnosing the connection pool's stalled waiter requires both the current implementation in `src/pool.py` and the test telemetry associated with `test_waiter_notified_on_return`. A search across repository history can easily return both an r17 test failure and an r18 reproducer pass. While both records are genuine, they answer distinct questions: one documents the defect that triggered the investigation, whereas the other evaluates a candidate patch. Before choosing an index structure or a similarity metric, a system must specify what the agent's next decision demands and what guarantees a returned record actually establishes.

::: {#dfn-episodic-retrieval-contract .callout-definition title="Retrieval contract"}

A ***retrieval contract***\index{Retrieval contract!definition} specifies the information requested, the permitted scope and resource limits of the read, and the provenance, applicability, and completion information returned with its results.

1.  **Significance**: It ensures a bounded search result remains interpretable before that result enters the next model invocation. A misread or misattributed result exacts a double penalty in the cost per accepted task (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task): its tokens consume prompt budget and inference cost during the attempt, while the mistaken decision it induces drives down the acceptance probability.
2.  **Distinction**: Ranking algorithms merely score and order candidate items under a specific relevance heuristic. The retrieval contract establishes authorization boundaries, version constraints, serialization budgets, and explicit completion semantics.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Mistaking an empty result or a truncated scan for definitive proof that the requested data does not exist.

:::

This contract applies uniformly whether the agent executes an index search, a relational database query, or a direct filesystem read; it mandates no single storage layout or similarity threshold. It divides the work among three parties (@fig-vol3-retrieval-contract). The runtime sets the request's bounds, the retrieval service checks access and searches within them, and the result envelope reports status, provenance, and limitations before the runtime stages any evidence for the next model call.

::: {#fig-vol3-retrieval-contract fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Retrieval Contract**: The runtime sets the request's scope, version requirement, and limits; the model may propose search terms but cannot widen those bounds. The retrieval service checks access, searches, and excludes inapplicable versions, and the envelope reports what was searched and whether the operation completed, returned a partial result, or was unavailable. Only then does the runtime stage selected evidence, with its source and version labels, within the payload budget." fig-alt="Diagram with two cards across the top and a band below. The retrieval service card shows a grid of record tiles with a dashed purple frame labeled request bounds around part of it; tiles inside the frame are labeled r18 or r17, three r18 tiles are highlighted as hits, and two columns of gray tiles sit outside the frame; a key below the grid identifies a dashed tile as r17 excluded and a gray tile as outside scope. An arrow leads to the result envelope card, which lists searched scope and version r18, a status of complete, partial, or unavailable, limits with reason and continuation cursor, and three items each labeled path, range, r18, provenance. In the agent runtime band below, a set the bounds box (scope, version, limits; model proposes terms only) has an arrow up to the request bounds frame, an arrow from the envelope leads down to a stage evidence box holding two items in a payload budget bar, and an arrow leads on to next model call."}
![](images/svg/episodic_memory_stack.svg)
:::

### The bounded request {#sec-vol3-persistent-query-tuple}

A raw information need such as "find the notification logic" underspecifies the retrieval operation. It leaves undefined whether the caller requires the active workspace, an earlier Git revision, or a diff between them; it says nothing about which repositories the principal may access; and it ignores how many tokens the caller's remaining context window can accommodate. As summarized in @tbl-vol3-query-tuple, framing retrieval as a bounded request separates these operational constraints from the underlying index mechanics.

| Request field                    | Meaning in the repair task                                                                 | Boundary it establishes                                                               |
|:---------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Query or information need        | Locate the waiter-notification implementation or the recorded reproducer result            | The requested match or observation, not a promise that it exists                      |
| Authorized scope and principal   | The designated repair workspace and the identity under which it is read                    | The runtime checks permitted paths and records; a scope string alone grants no access |
| Version or freshness requirement | Read r18, compare r17 with r18, or read the current source under stated snapshot semantics | Which state can answer the question                                                   |
| Result-count and payload limits  | Bound returned items and their serialized representation                                   | Count and content size are separate limits                                            |
| Execution limits                 | Deadline and supported bounds on scans, expansions, or other search work                   | When to stop waiting or searching and report incomplete work                          |
| Optional filters                 | Restrict file type, symbol kind, or other relevant metadata                                | Narrow the information need without replacing authorization                           |

: **A bounded retrieval request**: The runtime can supply task-wide defaults, while each query specializes the information need within those limits. {#tbl-vol3-query-tuple}

A version requirement differs fundamentally from a wall-clock freshness heuristic. An index entry for revision r17 remains invalid as current r18 source code even if an indexing worker refreshed it seconds ago. Wall-clock TTLs merely trigger periodic reindexing, whereas explicit version tokens establish whether a cached representation strictly matches its underlying source snapshot. When the retrieval service cannot fulfill the requested version from its precomputed index, it must either fall back to an authorized direct read of the primary store or return an explicit incomplete status. @Sec-vol3-persistent-invalidation develops this trade-off once the index itself can lag its source.

Similarly, result-count, payload-size, and compute limits constrain different dimensions of system resource consumption. Ten complete source files consume far more serialized tokens than ten function docstrings, yet returning a single item might still require scanning millions of candidate records. The payload limit protects the caller's downstream context window, search-work budgets (such as graph traversal caps or posting-list scan limits) constrain retrieval service compute, and execution deadlines prevent the agent runtime from blocking indefinitely. Client timeouts must also propagate cancellation signals to the underlying storage engines; uncancelled background queries continue to consume backend resources and inflate total execution cost.

### The result envelope {#sec-vol3-persistent-result-envelope}

A production retrieval service returns metadata describing the search execution alongside the matching records. At the response level, the result envelope specifies the repository scope and snapshot revision actually searched, the terminal execution status, and any operational constraints that qualify the results:

- `complete` confirms that the declared search algorithm ran to conclusion under its stated semantics. It is a mechanical guarantee about the search performed, not a claim to have found every relevant fact.
- `partial` indicates that the operation halted before exhaustive evaluation, explicitly recording the abort reason (such as an expired deadline, an unavailable index partition, or an output payload cap).
- `unavailable` signals that the retrieval subsystem failed to return usable data, whether due to network partitions, authorization failures, or service crashes.

When an operation yields partial results or truncates output to respect payload limits, the envelope provides an opaque continuation cursor so subsequent bounded requests can resume paging without re-executing the entire query.

These statuses decide what the runtime may infer when a query returns zero hits, a rule this chapter calls the *absence rule*. An empty result proves nonexistence if and only if a fully completed exhaustive scan produced it, and even then only within the scanned scope and revision snapshot. A completed literal string search across the repository showing that a symbol does not occur in revision r18 meets this standard. A truncated or partial scan that returns zero matches proves nothing, because the target may reside in an unvisited partition. An approximate index (@sec-vol3-long-term-memory-vector-search) offers no absence guarantee even when it completes, because it deliberately skips most of the candidate space to save work; a result set that lacks the relevant record may reflect that skipped region rather than the record's absence from the corpus.

At the item level, every returned record carries structured metadata alongside its raw content: a persistent URI or path, byte or line ranges, the exact source commit or snapshot identifier, and a content hash of the returned bytes. When an item represents an empirical observation, such as a test execution log, the record must document the runtime configuration, environment variables, test revision, and terminal outcome. If an item stores a derived lesson or summary synthesized by an agent in an earlier session, its envelope must link to the primary records supporting that inference and flag its status as a derived model output. If the retrieval engine attaches a relevance score, it must name the algorithm that produced it (a lexical ranking function, a vector similarity, or a learned reranker, each developed later in this chapter). Ranking scores exist on their algorithm's internal scale; systems must not treat them as calibrated probabilities.

::: {#lst-vol3-result-envelope lst-cap="**A serialized result envelope**: The response-level fields report what was searched and how the search ended; each item carries its role, location, version, and hash beside its content. Symbolic values stand for settings and contents chosen by the runtime; the field names do not prescribe a storage API."}
```yaml
status: complete
scope: {workspace: repair, principal: repair-agent, source_snapshot: r18}
items:
  - role: source_record
    path: src/pool.py
    lines: [a, b]
    revision: r18
    content_hash: h18
    score: {method: lexical_rank, value: s}
    content: <slice of the return path>
  - role: observation
    test: test_waiter_notified_on_return
    revision: r17
    configuration: c17
    outcome: failed
    content: <recorded failure trace>
```
:::

In the connection-pool repair task, the staged payload might pair a slice of `src/pool.py` from revision `r18` with an error trace recorded under revision `r17`, as in @lst-vol3-result-envelope, where the fields outside the two `content` bodies count against the payload budget just as the bodies do. The r17 trace explains why the repair was initiated, but it provides zero evidence regarding the behavior of the r18 candidate. By packaging each record in an explicit envelope, the retrieval subsystem preserves these applicability distinctions across the boundary between persistent storage and the working context. Envelope labels, however, record provenance without certifying veracity. A cryptographic content hash verifies only that the byte sequence matches a specific snapshot; it does not validate the factual correctness of the text. Similarly, categorizing a record as user input or agent-written memory confers no administrative authority on any instructions embedded within that content.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The scope rule and the untrusted span are established in @sec-vol3-context-engineering-source-scope.
:::

### Evidence staging {#sec-vol3-persistent-quarantine}

The agent runtime, never the retrieval backend or an uncalibrated ranking score, determines which records enter the downstream prompt. The runtime curates evidence tailored to the immediate decision, preserves the source and version tags necessary for correct interpretation, and measures the token footprint of the serialized payload. Staging is where invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}) reaches the durable read boundary. The bound below the model is mechanical, because a runtime rule rather than the model or the ranker decides what is admitted, and the version labels it preserves are the evidence a later acceptance check needs to tell an `r17` observation from an `r18` one.

Retrieved records remain untrusted spans even when fetched from a local repository, because serialization that separates them from system instructions cannot stop the model from following text embedded in a record body, the hazard known as prompt injection.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Indirect prompt injection, delivered through retrieved documents and other observations an agent reads, is developed in @sec-vol3-security-injection-entry-points.
:::

Accurate payload accounting must measure the entire serialized envelope, including wrapper tags, source paths, version identifiers, and status headers, alongside the raw text bodies. Underestimating this structural overhead leads directly to context exhaustion. The ledger in notebook \ref{nbk-06-retrieval-payload-ledger} demonstrates how metadata overhead alters the number of complete records an agent can stage within a fixed prompt allocation.

```{python}
#| label: lego-06-retrieval-payload-ledger
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SERIALIZED RETRIEVAL PAYLOAD LEDGER
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-06-retrieval-payload-ledger
# │ Goal: Bound complete retrieved records after output and envelope reserves.
# │ Show: Retrieval allowance, record capacity, payload used, and remainder.
# │ How: Explicit hypothetical token counts; no hardware or tokenizer claim.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_math

class RetrievalPayloadLedger:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario assumptions, in serialized tokens) ─────────────
    capacity = 32_768
    output_reserve = 2_048
    other_input = 24_576
    envelope = 128
    body = 512
    metadata = 64

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    allowance = capacity - output_reserve - other_input
    record = body + metadata
    records = (allowance - envelope) // record
    used = envelope + records * record
    remaining = allowance - used
    body_only = allowance // body  # records a body-only limit would admit
    body_only_used = envelope + body_only * record
    overshoot = body_only_used - allowance

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(allowance == 6_144, "retrieval allowance")
    check(record == 576 and records == 10, "complete record capacity")
    check(used == 5_888 and remaining == 256, "complete serialized payload")
    check(used <= allowance < used + record, "one additional record cannot fit")
    check(body_only == 12 and body_only_used == 7_040 and overshoot == 896, "body-only limit overshoots")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    capacity_str = fmt_int(capacity)
    output_reserve_str = fmt_int(output_reserve)
    other_input_str = fmt_int(other_input)
    envelope_str = fmt_int(envelope)
    body_str = fmt_int(body)
    metadata_str = fmt_int(metadata)
    record_str = fmt_int(record)
    records_str = fmt_int(records)
    remaining_str = fmt_int(remaining)
    allowance_str = fmt_int(allowance)
    body_only_str = fmt_int(body_only)
    body_only_used_str = fmt_int(body_only_used)
    overshoot_str = fmt_int(overshoot)
    overcount_str = fmt_int(body_only - records)
    allowance_math = fmt_math(rf"{capacity:,} - {output_reserve:,} - {other_input:,} = {allowance:,}")
    payload_math = fmt_math(rf"{envelope} + {records} \times {record} = {used:,}")
```

::: {#nbk-06-retrieval-payload-ledger .callout-notebook title="Making room for retrieved evidence"}

**Problem**: A hypothetical model call permits `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.capacity_str` tokens in total. Reserving `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.output_reserve_str` tokens for generation leaves the remainder for input. If baseline system prompts, tool schemas, and conversation history occupy `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.other_input_str` tokens, how many complete retrieval records can the prompt accommodate?

**Math**: The retrieval allowance is `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.allowance_math` tokens. Assume a `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.envelope_str`-token response envelope and records that each contain `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.body_str` body tokens plus `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.metadata_str` metadata tokens, giving `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.record_str` tokens per record.

The maximum number of complete records that fit is `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.records_str`. Staging these records alongside their envelope consumes `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.payload_math` tokens, leaving a remainder of `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.remaining_str` tokens, too few to hold another complete record.

A naive sizing policy that accounts only for raw document bodies would admit `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.body_only_str` records. When serialized with metadata and envelopes, however, those records require `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.body_only_used_str` tokens, overshooting the allocated retrieval budget by `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.overshoot_str` tokens.

**Systems insight**: Metadata and envelope framing consume context capacity just as surely as document bodies. In this configuration, each record dedicates `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.metadata_str` of its `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.record_str` tokens to provenance, causing a body-only heuristic to overcommit the prompt by `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.overcount_str` records. Systems runtimes must reserve capacity for output tokens and the global envelope first, then admit $\lfloor(\text{allowance} - \text{envelope})/(\text{body} + \text{metadata})\rfloor$ records, remembering that every token assigned to system instructions or tool definitions shrinks the retrieval allowance one for one.

:::

Because subword tokenizers (such as Byte-Pair Encoding) merge tokens across string boundaries, tokenizing text fragments in isolation and summing their counts yields an inaccurate total. Runtimes must measure token lengths on the final, fully serialized prompt structure using the target model's tokenizer. When a critical record exceeds the remaining budget, the runtime must not silently truncate the text. Instead, it should stage a syntactically coherent excerpt with explicit truncation markers, defer the item to a subsequent retrieval pass, or return an opaque handle that the model can resolve on demand.

Every staged token also incurs concrete inference engine overhead beyond occupying space in the context window. Retrieved context must be processed through the model's compute-intensive prefill phase and then pinned in accelerator memory as key-value (KV) cache tensors for the duration of the generation cycle or prefix cache retention window. Staging more records increases the token volume that the serving engine must process and retain, although the resulting prefill latency depends on the model, prefix reuse, and serving configuration. Every retained token counts against the resident-fit bound of the serving node's KV pool, so a generous staging policy reduces how many trajectories the node can serve concurrently.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The per-sequence footprint of key-value cache state, and how it limits the number of sequences a node can serve concurrently, is established in @sec-vol3-kvcache-geometry.
:::

::: {#chk-06-retrieval-contract .callout-checkpoint title="Interpreting a bounded result"}

Each question presents a retrieval outcome; decide what operational conclusions it licenses.

- [ ] **Stale excerpt**: A query for current source returns an r17 excerpt after the workspace reaches r18. Which historical diagnostic inferences remain valid, and what must happen before the excerpt informs an r18 edit?
- [ ] **Deadline vs. completion**: A search reaches its deadline with no matches. Which status does it return, and which conclusion that a completed literal scan of the same snapshot would support is unavailable here?
- [ ] **Payload estimate**: If per-record metadata doubled from the value in notebook \ref{nbk-06-retrieval-payload-ledger}, how many complete records would fit the same allowance, and what must the runtime measure before dispatching the call?

:::

The retrieval contract establishes the operational bounds, provenance requirements, and payload limits for each read, but it leaves open an architectural question, namely which component formulates the query. A runtime can predict needed evidence and pre-stage it before invoking the model, or it can equip the agent with search tools to probe the store interactively as discoveries unfold.

## Agentic Retrieval {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-agentic-retrieval}

When the repair agent diagnoses the stalled waiter in its connection pool, the runtime must decide how to supply the model with relevant evidence. Two distinct retrieval architectures address this challenge. In a pre-staged architecture, the runtime predicts which artifacts will be necessary (such as `src/pool.py`, `tests/test_pool.py`, and a stack trace from a prior run) and injects them directly into the prompt before model execution begins. In an agentic architecture, the runtime equips the model with bounded text search, file reading, and symbol-navigation tools, allowing the agent to locate notification logic, inspect the test harness, and follow cross-file references as intermediate discoveries dictate. Both architectures operate over the same underlying storage systems and share identical security boundaries. They differ in when the information need is resolved and which component formulates the retrieval queries.

Pre-staging implements standard **retrieval-augmented generation**\index{Retrieval-augmented generation!definition} (RAG), where the host system selects external documents and packages them alongside the prompt before inference begins [@lewis2020retrieval]. By contrast, **agentic retrieval**\index{Agentic retrieval!definition} delegates query formulation to the model during the execution loop, interleaving environment observations with subsequent reasoning and action steps [@yao2023react]. Autonomous systems designed for repository-scale software engineering [@jimenez2024swebench] rely heavily on this interactive paradigm, because providing the model with search and navigation commands shaped for code inspection proves far more adaptable than staging a single, static set of top-$\RetrievalCutoffCount$ retrieved passages up front [@yang2024sweagent]. Rather than mutually exclusive alternatives, these two patterns represent complementary policies operating over the same underlying data stores.

Pre-staging excels when the evidence required for the next decision is predictable. Loading `src/pool.py` and `tests/test_pool.py` directly into the prompt eliminates the latency and inference cost of an exploratory turn spent locating those files. However, pre-staging carries operational risks. It can consume scarce context capacity with irrelevant code, or conversely, miss transitively imported dependencies that only become apparent upon inspecting the source. Model-directed iterative search resolves this rigidity by allowing each discovery to reshape subsequent queries. For example, a failing assertion in a test file might name an internal helper function, prompting the agent to inspect that specific definition next. Interactive exploration, however, introduces its own failure modes. An agent can chase unpromising leads, execute redundant searches across familiar directories, or terminate its investigation prematurely before gathering sufficient evidence.

Before introducing an auxiliary index, such as an inverted text index or a vector store, an engineer should benchmark against a live-source baseline. Bounded substring searches and direct file reads inspect the target workspace directly on disk, introducing no external index that can lag behind ongoing edits. When a problem description already specifies exact filenames or literal error strings, these live-source primitives often supply all the retrieval capability the agent requires. Direct filesystem access, however, presents distinct systems trade-offs. Live reads observe whichever version of a file exists at the exact moment of execution; if concurrent processes modify the workspace, separate reads executed across successive turns can straddle modifications and observe inconsistent snapshots. Furthermore, raw literal searches locate character matches without semantic awareness, failing to distinguish an active symbol definition from an obsolete comment or an unrelated log message. An auxiliary index justifies its memory footprint, construction time, and synchronization overhead only when it measurably amortizes repetitive scanning costs across long trajectories, resolves vocabulary mismatches through semantic embeddings, or accelerates traversal over structural relationships such as call graphs derived from abstract syntax trees (ASTs). An evaluation must charge the cost of building and refreshing the index directly against its query-time savings, a charge the chapter prices at its end, once lexical, dense, and graph indexes are in hand (notebook \ref{nbk-06-storage-amplification}).

When an agent probes its environment, the runtime can optimize query execution through parallelism. A single model turn can emit several independent tool calls that the runtime batches or executes concurrently across threads; only queries that strictly depend on earlier observations must block for sequential resolution. @Tbl-vol3-long-term-memory-staged-vs-agentic summarizes the core trade-offs between runtime pre-staging and model-directed probing.

| Property               | Runtime pre-staging                                            | Model-directed probing                                         |
|:-----------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|
| Query selection        | Runtime policy selects evidence before model invocation        | Model formulates queries dynamically from prior observations   |
| Optimal scenario       | Likely evidence needs are predictable in advance               | Intermediate results dictate which question to ask next        |
| Computational overhead | Retrieval latency and staging cost prior to the call           | Search latency and extra inference rounds for query refinement |
| Characteristic failure | Missing transitively imported dependencies or bloating context | Chasing unproductive paths or terminating search prematurely   |
| Freshness guarantee    | Governed by source version and read contract at staging        | Governed by the same read contract at tool execution time      |
| Resource governance    | Bounded by staging timeouts and context-window capacity        | Bounded by per-call limits and trajectory-wide step budgets    |

: **Pre-staging and model-directed retrieval**: Query timing and ownership change between the two policies, while source applicability and runtime-enforced limits remain shared. {#tbl-vol3-long-term-memory-staged-vs-agentic}

Under both paradigms, the execution runtime retains authority over security boundaries and resource consumption. The model acts strictly as an untrusted query generator. It may propose a narrower search path, supply query strings, or request specific filters, but it can never expand the authorized workspace, assume a different principal identity, or increase its own resource ceilings. The runtime enforces these boundaries at the tool interface. Tool calling schemas define and constrain the supported request parameters, while tool execution results transmit truncation warnings, resource limits, and continuation tokens back to the agent.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Tool interface schemas that bound which request parameters a model may supply are developed in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-schemas.
:::

In production systems, these two strategies often merge into a tiered hybrid policy. The runtime pre-stages a compact workspace outline, an architectural summary, or persistent user preferences directly into the initial context window, giving the model immediate structural grounding. The agent then issues targeted tool calls to inspect specific function implementations or test traces only when those details become necessary. Evaluating such a hybrid design requires balancing the upfront token overhead of pre-staging against the inference latency and token expenditure of avoided tool turns.

The choice among a direct read, pre-staging, and directed probing follows from how much of the information need the task itself names. When the task names its targets, such as `src/pool.py` or a pinned note, a direct read stages exactly those records and spends no ranking or exploratory turn. When the needed evidence is predictable but unnamed, such as the tests that usually accompany a module, pre-staging captures it in one step at the price of some irrelevant tokens. When each needed item can be found only from the one before, as when a failing assertion names a helper whose definition names a lock, no pre-staged set can anticipate the chain, and model-directed probing pays one model round per dependent hop. A hybrid seeds the first hop by pre-staging or direct read and leaves the remaining hops to probing. Whichever component formulates the query, what comes back depends on the matching mechanism behind the read, whether lexical matching, learned similarity, or structural traversal, and each mechanism answers a different kind of information need.

## Lexical and Structural Retrieval {#sec-vol3-persistent-bm25}

When the repair agent investigates its stalled waiter, it faces distinct information needs: locating `tests/test_pool.py`, finding references to `test_waiter_notified_on_return`, and isolating the function enclosing a suspect synchronization statement. A well-designed retrieval contract does not force these varied tasks through a single mechanism. A known file path requires only a direct file read. A specific identifier calls for literal text search or symbol lookup. A broad symptom description requires ranking multiple candidate passages before the agent can decide which source files merit inspection.

### Exact lookup and lexical ranking {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-exact-lexical}

Exact path lookup retrieves a named object directly from an authorized repository snapshot. Literal text search scans for exact character sequences under declared matching rules such as case sensitivity and boundary delimiters. Neither mechanism interprets semantic role: a match on a test identifier might point to its primary definition, a passing mention in a comment, an import statement, or an entry in an archived failure log.

To support repeated lexical queries across large corpora without scanning every byte on disk, retrieval systems rely on an **inverted index**\index{Inverted index!definition} [@zobel2006inverted]. The index maps each distinct term to a postings list containing every document where the term appears. Beyond the document identifier, each posting typically stores the term's in-document frequency and position offsets. How source text maps into postings depends entirely on the index's analyzer. The analyzer determines token boundaries: whether it preserves full identifier tokens, splits `snake_case` and `camelCase` identifiers, normalizes letter case, or strips inflectional affixes through stemming. Consequently, a ranked match on an analyzed identifier behaves differently from an exact match on the raw string. When an agent requires an exact literal hit, it must either query an unanalyzed exact-match field or verify the returned source snippet directly.

When a query matches dozens or hundreds of candidates, ranking determines which documents enter the agent's bounded context window. The **BM25**\index{BM25!definition}[^fn-bm25-okapi-retrieval] scoring function balances three factors: term rarity across the corpus,[^fn-idf-term-rarity] sub-linear term frequency saturation within each candidate, and document-length normalization [@robertson2009bm25]:

$$
\operatorname{score}(\LexicalDocument,\LexicalQuery)=\sum_{\QueryWord\in \LexicalQuery}\operatorname{IDF}(\QueryWord)
\frac{\QueryWordFrequency(\QueryWord,\LexicalDocument)(\LexicalFrequencySaturation+1)}{\QueryWordFrequency(\QueryWord,\LexicalDocument)+\LexicalFrequencySaturation(1-\LexicalLengthNormalization+\LexicalLengthNormalization\lvert \LexicalDocument\rvert/\MeanDocumentLength)},
\qquad
\operatorname{IDF}(\QueryWord)=\ln\left(1+\frac{\IndexedDocumentCount-\QueryWordDocumentFrequency(\QueryWord)+0.5}{\QueryWordDocumentFrequency(\QueryWord)+0.5}\right).
$$ {#eq-vol3-bm25}

Here $\LexicalQuery$ contains the query terms, $\LexicalDocument$ is an indexed document, $\QueryWordFrequency(\QueryWord,\LexicalDocument)$ is the term frequency of $\QueryWord$ in $\LexicalDocument$, $\lvert \LexicalDocument\rvert$ is the document length in analyzer terms, and $\MeanDocumentLength$ is the collection's mean document length. The corpus contains $\IndexedDocumentCount$ documents in total, of which $\QueryWordDocumentFrequency(\QueryWord)$ contain query term $\QueryWord$. These lengths are analyzer counts, not the foundation model's token counts. These symbols are local to lexical ranking; in particular, $\LexicalDocument$ and $\LexicalLengthNormalization$ do not carry the meanings earlier chapters gave those letters. The tuning parameter $\LexicalFrequencySaturation>0$ controls term-frequency saturation. At a fixed document length, the frequency factor rises toward $\LexicalFrequencySaturation+1$ as $\QueryWordFrequency(\QueryWord,\LexicalDocument)$ grows, so each additional occurrence adds less to the score than the one before. The parameter $\LexicalLengthNormalization\in[0,1]$ modulates document-length normalization, with $\LexicalLengthNormalization=1$ fully penalizing documents proportional to their relative length and $\LexicalLengthNormalization=0$ disabling length normalization entirely. Because ranking depends on these mechanics, document chunk boundaries, analyzer choices, and parameter settings alter candidate scores even when the underlying source text remains unchanged.

[^fn-bm25-okapi-retrieval]: **BM25 (Best Match 25)**: The name records one weighting in the "Best Match" series of the Okapi retrieval system, built on the simple approximations to a two-Poisson model of term occurrence that @robertson1994simple derived. The formula survived decades of learned rankers because it needs no training data, only corpus statistics an index already keeps, which is why it remains the baseline a repository agent can deploy on the day its workspace is created. \index{BM25!Okapi origin}

[^fn-idf-term-rarity]: **Inverse Document Frequency (IDF)**: @sparckjones1972statistical proposed weighting a term by how few documents contain it, on the argument that a term shared by most documents cannot tell them apart. In a repository that argument favors exactly the tokens an agent searches for, such as a unique test name or error string, and discounts keywords every file shares, which is why a rare identifier ranks sharply under BM25 while a vague symptom description does not. \index{Inverse document frequency!origin}

```{python}
#| label: ltm-bm25-ranking-calc
#| echo: false
# What: Compare two lexical candidates, not their correctness.
# How: Apply the displayed BM25 variant to a hypothetical one-term query.
from math import log
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_ratio

class BM25Ranking:
    # 1. LOAD — stipulated corpus statistics, not measured repository data.
    documents = 100_000
    matching_documents = 5
    average_length = 400
    short_length, long_length = 80, 4_000
    short_frequency, long_frequency = 1, 6
    k1, b = 1.2, 0.75

    # 2. EXECUTE — lengths and frequencies are analyzer-term counts.
    idf = log(1 + (documents - matching_documents + 0.5) / (matching_documents + 0.5))
    short_normalizer = k1 * (1 - b + b * short_length / average_length)
    long_normalizer = k1 * (1 - b + b * long_length / average_length)
    short_score = idf * short_frequency * (k1 + 1) / (short_frequency + short_normalizer)
    long_score = idf * long_frequency * (k1 + 1) / (long_frequency + long_normalizer)

    # 3. GUARD — validate the scenario and the ordering being illustrated.
    check(0 < matching_documents <= documents, "Document frequencies must be valid")
    check(0 < short_frequency <= short_length, "Short-document counts must be valid")
    check(0 < long_frequency <= long_length, "Long-document counts must be valid")
    check(average_length > 0 and k1 > 0 and 0 <= b <= 1, "BM25 parameters must be valid")
    check(short_score > long_score > 0, "The example must rank the short candidate first")

    # 4. OUTPUT — presentation values for all displayed scenario quantities.
    documents_str = fmt_int(documents)
    matching_documents_str = fmt_int(matching_documents)
    average_length_str = fmt_int(average_length)
    short_length_str, long_length_str = fmt_int(short_length), fmt_int(long_length)
    short_frequency_str, long_frequency_str = fmt_int(short_frequency), fmt_int(long_frequency)
    k1_str, b_str = fmt_ratio(k1, precision=1), fmt_ratio(b, precision=2)
    idf_str = fmt_ratio(idf, precision=3)
    short_score_str = fmt_ratio(short_score, precision=2)
    long_score_str = fmt_ratio(long_score, precision=2)
    short_normalizer_str = fmt_ratio(short_normalizer, precision=2)
    long_normalizer_str = fmt_ratio(long_normalizer, precision=1)
```

::: {#exmp-06-quantitative-bm25-score-dynamics-on .callout-example title="A higher lexical score is a ranking decision"}
**Scenario**: Consider a hypothetical index of `{python} BM25Ranking.documents_str` documents with a mean length of `{python} BM25Ranking.average_length_str` analyzer terms. A single query term appears in `{python} BM25Ranking.matching_documents_str` documents. With $\LexicalFrequencySaturation=$ `{python} BM25Ranking.k1_str` and $\LexicalLengthNormalization=$ `{python} BM25Ranking.b_str`, its inverse document frequency is `{python} BM25Ranking.idf_str`.

**Analysis**: A short candidate contains `{python} BM25Ranking.short_length_str` terms and `{python} BM25Ranking.short_frequency_str` occurrence of the query term; a long candidate contains `{python} BM25Ranking.long_length_str` terms and `{python} BM25Ranking.long_frequency_str` occurrences. The length term $\LexicalFrequencySaturation(1-\LexicalLengthNormalization+\LexicalLengthNormalization\lvert \LexicalDocument\rvert/\MeanDocumentLength)$ in the denominator of @eq-vol3-bm25 is `{python} BM25Ranking.short_normalizer_str` for the short candidate but `{python} BM25Ranking.long_normalizer_str` for the long one, so the long candidate's extra occurrences are divided by a far larger denominator. Substituting these counts into the scoring rule gives `{python} BM25Ranking.short_score_str` for the short candidate and `{python} BM25Ranking.long_score_str` for the long candidate. Repetition alone does not determine their order: saturation and length normalization outweigh the long candidate's additional occurrences.

**Systems lesson**: Rank orders candidates for inspection. If the short candidate is a comment while the long one holds the implementation, the agent still needs source inspection or structural information, and choosing whole files rather than functions as documents would change both scores.
:::

### Structural evidence {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-structural-evidence}

Lexical matches identify raw text occurrences. **Structural retrieval**\index{Structural retrieval!definition} distinguishes program organization: the enclosing function, type declarations, lexical scopes, and identifiers in call expressions. A parser translates source text into abstract syntax trees with explicit spans, while symbol resolution and semantic analysis establish directed relationships between definitions and call sites. While parsing a call expression identifies the call site syntactically, resolving which concrete implementation executes at runtime requires interprocedural analysis.

During the connection-pool repair, a structural query can return the entire function containing a notification call in `src/pool.py` rather than an arbitrary fragment, and a reference query can subsequently identify its callers across the codebase. Static coverage depends on language semantics, dependencies, and build configuration; dynamic dispatch, reflection, generated code, and cross-process calls frequently escape static resolution. In a structural index, a missing edge indicates a gap in static coverage rather than an unreachable path, while a static call edge records a potential invocation rather than an executed one. The two representations see the pool's sources differently (@fig-vol3-lexical-vs-ast). A lexical index finds the term `notify` in the pool source and the r17 failure log alike, whereas a structural index records that the waiter test calls the pool's return method, which in turn calls the notification, a caller-callee chain that string matching cannot recover.

::: {#fig-vol3-lexical-vs-ast fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Occurrences vs. Relationships**: A lexical index (A) maps each analyzed term to postings of documents and frequencies, so the term notify matches the pool source and the r17 failure log alike. A structural index (B) records parsed containment and resolved calls, here from the waiter test to the pool's return method and on to its notification call. Its coverage is declared rather than complete, because a dynamic call can leave a target unresolved." fig-alt="Two stacked panels. Panel A, lexical index, shows three quoted terms, notify, waiter, and return, each with an arrow to two postings naming a file and a term frequency; the notify row and its postings src/pool.py 2 and r17.log 1 are highlighted and labeled source and failure log alike, with a note that a match is an occurrence, not a relationship. Panel B, structural index, shows the file tests/test_pool.py containing the function test_waiter_notified_on_return and the file src/pool.py containing pool return method and _available.notify(). A CALLS arrow links the test function to the return method, a second CALLS arrow links the return method to _available.notify(), and a dashed arrow labeled CALLS with a question mark leads from the test function to a dashed box labeled dynamic call: target unknown."}
![](images/svg/symbol_graph_topology.svg)
:::

@Tbl-vol3-lexical-vs-ast-table separates the questions these methods answer. Lexical indexes can carry path and symbol metadata, but text matching alone establishes no semantic relationship.

| **Information need**                              | **Suitable starting method**                      | **What the result establishes**                                                    |
|:--------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Read a known path or locate a literal identifier  | Direct source read or declared exact-match search | The requested content or occurrences within the searched scope and version         |
| Find likely relevant documents from query terms   | Lexical ranking such as BM25                      | Candidate order under the analyzer, document boundaries, and scoring rule          |
| Find an enclosing function or resolved references | Syntax or semantic index with declared coverage   | Parsed boundaries or analysis-derived relationships, not complete runtime behavior |

: **Exact, Lexical, and Structural Retrieval**: Choose the method according to the information required, then interpret its result within the method's coverage. {#tbl-vol3-lexical-vs-ast-table}

### Search scope {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-search-scope}

Restricting an initial probe to `src/pool.py` and `tests/test_pool.py` focuses the evidence and limits noise, provided the retrieval interface explicitly reports that bounded scope; a subsequent probe can widen the scope to investigate callers across the repository.

Filtering and ranking interact directly. A service that selects its top-ranked candidates globally and only then discards those outside the requested paths (post-filtering) can easily return an empty set while eligible matches sit farther down the global ranking. Restricting candidates before final scoring (pre-filtering) avoids this loss, as does continuing postings traversal until the requested quota of filtered documents is filled. When query budgets or latency limits terminate the search early, the result remains partial.

Choosing the evaluation order is a cost-based optimization decision analogous to access path selection in relational database optimizers [@selinger1979access].[^fn-selectivity-optimizer-memory] The decision balances the filter's selectivity against the rarity of the query terms. A selective filter, such as one that isolates two files in a repository of thousands, favors pre-filtering candidate documents and evaluating BM25 scores only on the survivors. Conversely, a broad filter paired with a rare identifier favors scoring first, because the rare term's postings list is already short, provided the search engine continues scanning until enough eligible results remain. This trade-off reemerges with even sharper operational hazards when searching vector proximity graphs (@sec-vol3-persistent-dense-retrieval).

[^fn-selectivity-optimizer-memory]: **Cost-Based Access Path Selection**: The System R optimizer chose among index scans, sequential scans, and join orders by estimating each predicate's selectivity and the pages each plan would touch [@selinger1979access]. A retrieval gateway faces the same estimate with a scope filter as the predicate and a postings list or vector index as the access path, and a wrong estimate costs either a scan of the whole corpus or an empty result that looks like absence. \index{Query optimization!selectivity}

### Vocabulary mismatch {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-vocabulary-mismatch}

Exact and structural lookups succeed when the agent already possesses informative names or file locations. Early in an investigation, however, the agent may know only an observed symptom: “a connection is returned, but another caller keeps waiting,” phrased in words the source code never uses. This is the **vocabulary mismatch**\index{Vocabulary mismatch!definition} problem, where system designers and users formulate identical concepts using distinct vocabularies [@furnas1987vocabulary]. Heuristic techniques like identifier splitting, synonym expansion, or query reformulation can recover some lexical matches; once an exploratory search identifies a concrete test name, literal lookup is far more direct than further conceptual search.

When lexical heuristics still leave the candidate set inadequate, the agent needs a representation that maps descriptive prose to differently worded source implementations, along with hybrid rankers that combine dense semantic similarity with exact lexical precision without mistaking similarity for verification.

## Dense and Hybrid Retrieval {#sec-vol3-persistent-dense-retrieval}

When an agent investigates a bug report describing a caller that hangs indefinitely, lexical search across the repository can easily rank the critical return path in `src/pool.py` low or miss it entirely. The line that matters executes `notify()`, but the report describes a caller that keeps waiting. Dense retrieval supplies a complementary candidate-generation mechanism, using learned representations to match a query against records that share underlying meaning rather than literal tokens. Because dense and lexical methods fail in different places, production systems usually run both and combine their rankings, which is where this section ends.

### Dense retrieval {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-dense-retrieval}

**Dense retrieval**\index{Dense retrieval!definition} encodes a query and each searchable record as vectors using a learned model, ranking records by vector similarity.[^fn-vector-space-lineage] In a bi-encoder architecture, records are embedded offline before a request arrives, leaving only the query to be encoded online at request time [@karpukhin2020dense]. This separation removes heavy embedding inference from the critical query path. However, offline encoding remains an ongoing operational requirement. Newly inserted or modified records require fresh vector generation, and upgrading or fine-tuning the underlying encoder invalidates the entire index, demanding a complete corpus re-embedding.

[^fn-vector-space-lineage]: **Vector Space Model**: Ranking documents by the angle between a query vector and each document vector predates learned encoders; @salton1975vector represented every document as a vector of term weights and scored it by cosine similarity. Dense retrieval keeps the geometry and replaces sparse, interpretable term weights with learned components, which is what lets it bridge vocabulary and also why no single component explains a match. \index{Vector space model!origin}

The distance metric is defined by the interaction between the encoder and index configurations. For example, inner product search is mathematically identical to cosine similarity when vectors are unit-normalized ($\ell_2 = 1.0$), which shifts the computational cost of vector normalization to indexing time rather than paying for vector division on the query path. Neither metric, however, produces a calibrated probability that a candidate record answers the agent's question; they represent uncalibrated geometric affinities.

In the software repair task, a dense retriever can readily connect the symptom of a waiting caller to the return-and-notify implementation, yielding a promising candidate for inspection rather than proof of a defect. The semantic abstraction that bridges vocabulary gaps, however, can also blur fine syntactic distinctions on which code execution depends. Consider a concrete case in `src/pool.py`: the return path invokes `self._available.notify()`, the shutdown routine invokes `self._available.notify_all()`, and acquisition invokes `self._available.wait(timeout)`. All three statements share the same condition variable, module context, and conceptual vocabulary of thread synchronization. Consequently, an encoder often maps all three to neighboring points in vector space when queried about thread unblocking. Their operational semantics are nonetheless entirely distinct: one wakes a single waiter, another wakes every waiter, and the third blocks. An exact lexical search for `notify(` isolates the call site immediately, and BM25 assigns the rare identifier a high inverse document frequency (IDF). The systems challenge is therefore determining which retrieval mechanism surfaces the precise evidence the workload requires.

### Exact and approximate vector search {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-vector-search}

An **exact vector scan**\index{Exact vector scan!definition} scores every vector in the eligible search set under the chosen distance metric. It serves as the baseline ground truth for measuring what an approximate search misses, and it remains a practical serving method whenever the eligible candidate set is small.

The fundamental resource requirements of an exact scan follow directly from dimensional arithmetic, independent of any specific hardware architecture. Let $\EligibleVectorCount$ be the number of eligible vectors, $\EmbeddingDimension$ their dimension, and $\ElementStorageSize$ the storage width in bytes per component; like the ranking symbols before them, these letters are local to vector search. Traversing the stored vectors requires streaming $\EligibleVectorCount \EmbeddingDimension\ElementStorageSize$ bytes from memory, so on a memory system that sustains bandwidth $\Bandwidth$ one scan takes at least $\EligibleVectorCount \EmbeddingDimension\ElementStorageSize/\Bandwidth$. Counting two floating-point operations per multiply-accumulate operation, dot-product scoring requires approximately $2\EligibleVectorCount \EmbeddingDimension$ FLOPs. These totals account only for the vector inner products; they exclude the latency of query embedding, top-$\RetrievalCutoffCount$ heap maintenance, and fetching the full record payloads from persistent storage.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The roofline model and the ridge point that separates bandwidth-bound from compute-bound work are developed in @sec-vol3-appendix-inference-roofline.
:::

```{python}
#| label: lego-06-memory-bandwidth-and-latency-floor
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ EXACT VECTOR SCAN: INTENSITY AND BANDWIDTH FLOOR (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-06-memory-bandwidth-and-latency-floor
# │ Goal: Show that an exact dot-product scan is bandwidth-bound on a host.
# │ Show: 1 FLOP/byte at FP16 vs a 20 FLOP/byte host ridge; 307.2 ms floor.
# │ How: Hypothetical corpus; host bandwidth and peak rate from the registry.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Hardware
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_FP16, GB, GFLOP, byte, flop, millisecond, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_arithmetic_intensity, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_flop_rate, fmt_flops, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_time

class VectorScanLatencyFloor:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Hypothetical corpus; host from the registry) ─────────────
    host = Hardware.Cloud.ReferenceCPU
    n_vectors = 10_000_000
    d_dim = 768
    bytes_per_val = BYTES_FP16
    n_probes = 20  # stipulated searches in one trajectory
    n_filtered = 10_000  # stipulated eligible set after a selective scope filter
    t_budget = 10 * millisecond  # stipulated per-search latency budget

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Bytes, FLOPs, intensity, and the two time floors) ────
    bw = host.memory.bandwidth
    peak = host.compute.peak_flops
    footprint = n_vectors * d_dim * bytes_per_val
    flops_total = 2 * n_vectors * d_dim * flop
    intensity = (flops_total / footprint).to(flop / byte)
    ridge = (peak / bw).to(flop / byte)
    t_mem = (footprint / bw).to(millisecond)
    t_arith = (flops_total / peak).to(millisecond)
    t_probes = (n_probes * t_mem).to(second)
    t_filtered = (n_filtered * d_dim * bytes_per_val / bw).to(millisecond)
    n_budget = int((t_budget * bw / (d_dim * bytes_per_val)).to("").magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(footprint.to(GB).magnitude - 15.36) < 1e-9, "vector bytes")
    check(abs(flops_total.to(GFLOP).magnitude - 15.36) < 1e-9, "scan FLOPs")
    check(abs(intensity.magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-12, "one FLOP per byte at FP16")
    check(ridge > 10 * intensity, "scan sits far below the host ridge")
    check(t_mem > 10 * t_arith, "bandwidth term dominates")
    check(t_filtered < t_budget < t_mem, "filtered scan meets the budget; full scan does not")
    check(n_filtered < n_budget < n_vectors, "budget crossover lies between the two sets")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_vectors_str = fmt_int(n_vectors)
    d_dim_str = fmt_int(d_dim)
    width_str = fmt_memory(bytes_per_val, unit=byte, precision=0)
    footprint_str = fmt_memory(footprint, unit=GB, precision=2)
    work_str = fmt_flops(flops_total, unit=GFLOP, precision=2)
    intensity_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(intensity, precision=0)
    ridge_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(ridge, precision=0)
    bw_str = fmt_bandwidth(bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    peak_str = fmt_flop_rate(peak, precision=0)
    t_mem_str = fmt_time(t_mem, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_arith_str = fmt_time(t_arith, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    n_probes_str = fmt_int(n_probes)
    t_probes_str = fmt_time(t_probes, unit=second, precision=1)
    n_filtered_str = fmt_int(n_filtered)
    t_filtered_str = fmt_time(t_filtered, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    t_budget_str = fmt_time(t_budget, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    n_budget_str = fmt_int(round(n_budget, -3), approx=True)
```

::: {#nbk-06-memory-bandwidth-and-latency-floor .callout-notebook title="Why an exact vector scan is bandwidth-bound"}
**Problem**: Consider a hypothetical searchable set of `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.n_vectors_str` vectors, each with `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.d_dim_str` components stored in FP16 at `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.width_str` per component, held in the main memory of a reference server CPU. Which resource limits one exact dot-product scan, and what floor does it set?

**Math**: Multiply the vector count by the dimension and component width:

$$
\EligibleVectorCount \EmbeddingDimension\ElementStorageSize = 10^7 \times 768 \times 2\ \text{bytes}.
$$

The raw vectors occupy `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.footprint_str`. Counting two FLOPs per multiply-add gives $2\EligibleVectorCount \EmbeddingDimension$, or `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.work_str` per scan. Arithmetic intensity, the FLOPs performed per byte moved from memory, is therefore $2\EligibleVectorCount \EmbeddingDimension/(\EligibleVectorCount \EmbeddingDimension\ElementStorageSize) = 2/\ElementStorageSize$, which is `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.intensity_str` at FP16 whatever the corpus size or dimension. The reference host delivers `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.peak_str` and `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.bw_str`, a ridge point of `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.ridge_str`, the intensity below which memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic limits the rate. The scan sits far below the ridge, so bandwidth sets its floor. Streaming the vectors takes at least `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.t_mem_str`, while the arithmetic alone would take `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.t_arith_str`. A trajectory that issues `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.n_probes_str` such searches spends at least `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.t_probes_str` moving vectors. Because the floor is linear in the eligible count, a scope filter that leaves `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.n_filtered_str` vectors has a streaming floor of `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.t_filtered_str`. A `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.t_budget_str` search budget sets an optimistic maximum of `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.n_budget_str` vectors on this host before accounting for the rest of the request.

**Systems insight**: The intensity of an exact scan is fixed by the component width, so added arithmetic never speeds it up, and an accelerator's higher ridge leaves it bandwidth-bound there too. The levers are fewer bytes per vector (compression) and fewer vectors touched (a narrower eligible set or an approximate index). The bandwidth floor screens out exact scans that cannot meet the search budget. When that floor fits, benchmark the complete request, including query encoding, top-$\RetrievalCutoffCount$ selection, and record fetches. Choose an exact scan when its measured request latency meets the budget; an approximate index must justify its maintenance cost and recall loss against that baseline.
:::
