The memory-bandwidth limit behind output-bound latency (principle \ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}) therefore reappears in retrieval, because an exact scan, like a decode step, performs only a few operations for each byte it streams. The analysis also establishes where an exact scan remains the right architectural choice. When selective metadata filters restrict the search space to thousands of eligible vectors, an exact scan streams megabytes rather than gigabytes, reducing the streaming floor to sub-millisecond times without the operational overhead of graph maintenance or quantization codebooks. Whether the complete request meets its latency budget still requires measurement. Furthermore, because an exact scan provides perfect recall under the chosen distance metric, it serves as the essential ground truth for evaluating any approximate index.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_ltm_margin_scan_crossover.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Log-log line chart of exact scan time against eligible vectors. A straight rising line passes a green dot at 10,000 vectors and 0.31 ms and a red dot at 10 million vectors and 307.2 ms. A dashed horizontal line marks a 10 ms budget and crosses the scan line near 326,000 vectors."}

*The exact-scan streaming floor grows with eligible vectors; the search budget sets an optimistic candidate ceiling.*
:::

When candidate sets grow into millions of vectors and queries must return within tight latency budgets, scanning the entire corpus becomes prohibitive. **Approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search**\index{Approximate nearest-neighbor search!definition}[^fn-ann-dimensionality-curse] trades mathematical exactness for orders-of-magnitude reductions in latency and memory traffic, pruning the search space at the cost of occasionally missing true nearest neighbors. Systems cut memory traffic in one of two fundamental ways: by traversing a proximity graph to evaluate only a tiny fraction of the vector population, or by partitioning the space and compressing vector representations with quantization codes.

[^fn-ann-dimensionality-curse]: **Approximate Nearest Neighbors**: Exact nearest-neighbor structures that work well in two or three dimensions degrade toward a full scan as dimension grows, the curse of dimensionality. @indyk1998approximate relaxed the problem to returning a point within a factor of the true nearest distance and showed, through locality-sensitive hashing, that the relaxation admits sublinear query time. Every ANN index an agent uses makes the same bargain, so its misses are part of the contract, measured as recall, never a defect to be tuned away. \index{Approximate nearest-neighbor search!origin}

A **hierarchical navigable small-world (HNSW)**\index{HNSW!definition} index organizes high-dimensional vectors into a multi-layer proximity graph [@malkov2018efficient]. Layer 0 contains every vector in the dataset. Each inserted vector is also assigned a maximum layer $\ell = \lfloor -\ln \HnswLevelDraw \cdot \HnswLevelNormalization \rfloor$, where $\HnswLevelDraw$ is drawn uniformly from $(0, 1]$ and $\HnswLevelNormalization = 1 / \ln \HnswMaximumConnectionCount$, with $\HnswMaximumConnectionCount$ defining the maximum number of bidirectional connections per node per layer. The assignment gives each vector probability $\HnswMaximumConnectionCount^{-\HnswLayerIndex}$ of reaching layer $\HnswLayerIndex$ or above, so each layer holds roughly $1/\HnswMaximumConnectionCount$ as many nodes as the one beneath it, an exponentially thinning hierarchy that mirrors the express transit lanes of a skip list [@pugh1990skip]. Traversal begins at an entry point in the sparsest top layer, greedily hopping to whichever neighbor minimizes distance to the query vector $\SearchQueryEmbedding$. When no neighbor yields further progress, the search drops down to that node's counterpart in the next layer and resumes the greedy walk. Upon reaching layer 0, the traversal switches from greedy routing to a beam search that maintains a priority queue of the $\HnswSearchBeamWidth$ closest candidates discovered so far. The search terminates when the closest unexplored neighbor cannot improve the current candidate set, returning the top $\RetrievalCutoffCount$ vectors. The parameter $\HnswSearchBeamWidth$ serves as the primary query-time recall knob. A vector the beam never visits cannot be returned (@fig-vol3-hnsw-routing), so widening the beam evaluates more distances and recovers more true neighbors at the cost of higher query latency.

Constructing an HNSW graph requires executing this layered search for every incoming vector and establishing bidirectional links to its nearest neighbors in each layer. This graph topology incurs substantial memory overhead beyond the raw vectors. Deletions are harder still, because severing a node without reconstructing edge paths among its neighbors risks partitioning the graph and stranding downstream vectors. Production systems therefore mark a deleted node with a tombstone, an exclusion marker that hides it from results while its links stay in place, and @sec-vol3-persistent-invalidation examines how the cost of that compromise compounds.

::: {#fig-vol3-hnsw-routing fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Searching an HNSW Graph**: Each upper layer holds a geometrically smaller subset of the vectors. The query enters at the top, hops greedily toward $\SearchQueryEmbedding$ until no neighbor is closer, and drops a layer from that node. In layer 0 the walk widens into a beam of width $\HnswSearchBeamWidth$ that visits more nodes than it returns and yields the best $\RetrievalCutoffCount$. A vector the beam never visits cannot be returned, which is where approximate search misses come from." fig-alt="Three stacked tilted planes labeled layer 2 (few vectors), layer 1 (more vectors), and layer 0 (every vector, up to M links each), drawn over one shared point layout so each upper layer shows a subset of the same vectors, with a dashed query marker q at the same position in every plane. In layer 2 a blue arrow hops from the entry point to a node nearer q, and a dashed arrow labeled no closer neighbor: drop falls straight down to the same node in layer 1; after a second hop, another dashed arrow labeled drop: beam starts here falls to layer 0. In layer 0 green links and outlined nodes mark the nodes the beam visited around q and three filled green nodes mark the returned nodes; the remaining gray nodes were never visited. A key identifies greedy hop, visited by beam with width ef search, returned best k, and never visited."}
![](images/svg/hnsw_hierarchical_routing.svg)
:::

Rather than navigating a graph over full-precision vectors, an inverted file index combined with **product quantization**\index{Product quantization!definition} (IVF-PQ) reduces memory traffic by partitioning the vector space and lossily compressing the stored representations [@jegou2011product], with an offline build pipeline and an online query pipeline (@fig-vol3-ivf-pq). During index construction, coarse $\Glyph{k}$-means clusters the corpus into $\CoarseCellCount$ Voronoi cells (each cell is the region of vectors nearer its centroid than any other centroid), each backed by an inverted list of vector identifiers. At query time, the system computes the distance from the uncompressed query vector to all $\CoarseCellCount$ coarse centroids and evaluates only the vectors residing in the $\ProbedCellCount$ closest cells.

Product quantization then compresses every stored vector. It splits the $\EmbeddingDimension$ dimensions into $\PqSubvectorCount$ distinct subvectors of dimension $\EmbeddingDimension/\PqSubvectorCount$. For each subspace, $\Glyph{k}$-means trains a codebook of 256 centroids, allowing any subvector to be represented by a single one-byte index $\PqCentroidCode_j \in [0, 255]$ indicating its nearest centroid. Storing a compressed vector therefore requires only $\PqSubvectorCount$ bytes. At query time, the uncompressed query vector $\SearchQueryEmbedding$ is segmented into the same $\PqSubvectorCount$ subspaces. The runtime precomputes an asymmetric distance lookup table $\text{LUT}[\PqSubspaceIndex, \PqCentroidCode]$, which stores the squared Euclidean distance between the query's $\PqSubspaceIndex$-th subvector and centroid $\PqCentroidCode$ in subspace $\PqSubspaceIndex$. The approximate distance between the query $\SearchQueryEmbedding$ and a stored quantized vector $\StoredIndexVector$ with codes $\PqCentroidCode_1, \dots, \PqCentroidCode_{\PqSubvectorCount}$ reduces to summing table lookups:

$$
\PqApproximateDistance(\SearchQueryEmbedding, \StoredIndexVector) = \sum_{j=1}^{\PqSubvectorCount} \text{LUT}[\PqSubspaceIndex, \PqCentroidCode_j].
$$ {#eq-vol3-pq-adc}

@Eq-vol3-pq-adc transforms a bandwidth-bound $\EmbeddingDimension$-component dot product into $\PqSubvectorCount$ single-byte reads and table lookups. Because the lookup table is small enough to stay in processor cache, each scored vector costs $\PqSubvectorCount$ bytes of memory traffic instead of $\EmbeddingDimension\ElementStorageSize$, a reduction by the factor $\EmbeddingDimension\ElementStorageSize/\PqSubvectorCount$ in exactly the term that bounded the exact scan. The parameter $\ProbedCellCount$ balances recall against the number of cells scanned, while the subvector count $\PqSubvectorCount$ trades distance fidelity against bytes per code. Systems commonly recover distance accuracy by re-scoring a short candidate list against full-precision vectors stored on secondary media or remote memory. This architecture scales gracefully to billions of vectors on accelerators [@johnson2019billion]. However, the quantization codebooks and coarse centroids are calibrated on the vector distribution present during index construction; as the corpus drifts or if the embedding model changes, quantization error compounds until the index is retrained.

::: {#fig-vol3-ivf-pq fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**IVF-PQ Build and Query**: At build time each stored vector is split into $\PqSubvectorCount = 64$ subvectors, each replaced by the one-byte index of its nearest centroid in that subspace's codebook, and the code is appended to the inverted list of its nearest coarse cell. At query time the full-precision query selects the $\ProbedCellCount$ nearest cells, fills a table of distances to every subspace centroid, and scores each stored code with $\PqSubvectorCount$ table lookups. Sizes follow the exact-scan notebook's corpus." fig-alt="Three tiers. The top band, labeled build, shows the stored vector x of 768 FP16 dimensions as a bar of 64 subvector segments with segment j highlighted; an arrow leads down to codebook j, a row of centroid squares with one highlighted, and a second arrow labeled c j leads down to the matching cell of the code for x, a short, thin row of 64 one-byte indices, much smaller than the vector bar, whose cell j sits directly below subvector j, noted as 24 times fewer bytes than the FP16 vector. An arrow appends the code to cell C. The middle row shows inverted lists for cells 1 through 4 and cell C, each holding short code entries, with cells 3 and C shaded blue; a key swatch below the cells labels the blue shading probed: n probe nearest to q. The bottom band, labeled query, shows query q in full precision, choose cells, a lookup-table grid labeled LUT j, c of 64 by 256 squared distances with one cell highlighted per row, and score each code as the sum over j of LUT j, c j with 64 lookups and adds; an arrow labeled scan codes runs from cell C into the scoring box."}
![](images/svg/episodic_ivf_pq.svg)
:::

```{python}
#| label: lego-06-ann-footprint
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ANN INDEX FOOTPRINT (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-vol3-ann-tradeoffs and the cost line before it.
# │ Goal: Size HNSW links and PQ codes for the exact-scan notebook's corpus.
# │ Show: 2.56 GB of links beside 15.36 GB of vectors; 0.64 GB of codes (24x).
# │ How: Stipulated M=32 links of 8 bytes; m=64 one-byte PQ subcodes.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_FP32, GB, KB, byte
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_multiple

class AnnFootprint:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Corpus from the exact-scan notebook; stipulated index shape) ─
    n = VectorScanLatencyFloor.n_vectors
    d = VectorScanLatencyFloor.d_dim
    raw = VectorScanLatencyFloor.footprint
    links_per_node = 32
    link_bytes = 8 * byte
    pq_subvectors = 64
    pq_centroids = 256
    code_bytes_per_sub = 1 * byte
    lut_entry = BYTES_FP32

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    graph = n * links_per_node * link_bytes
    codes = n * pq_subvectors * code_bytes_per_sub
    ratio = (raw / codes).to("").magnitude
    lut = (pq_subvectors * pq_centroids * lut_entry).to(KB)
    sub_dim = d // pq_subvectors

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(d % pq_subvectors == 0, "subvectors tile the dimension")
    check(abs(graph.to(GB).magnitude - 2.56) < 1e-9, "graph links")
    check(abs(codes.to(GB).magnitude - 0.64) < 1e-9, "PQ codes")
    check(ratio == 24, "FP16 vectors to PQ codes")
    check(abs(lut.magnitude - 65.536) < 1e-9, "lookup table size (64 x 256 x 4 bytes)")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    links_str = fmt_int(links_per_node)
    graph_str = fmt_memory(graph, unit=GB, precision=2)
    total_hnsw_str = fmt_memory(raw + graph, unit=GB, precision=2)
    code_str = fmt_int(pq_subvectors)
    sub_dim_str = fmt_int(sub_dim)
    codes_str = fmt_memory(codes, unit=GB, precision=2)
    ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(ratio, precision=0)
    lut_str = fmt_memory(lut, unit=KB, precision=1)
```

These structural trade-offs become concrete when sized against the 10-million-vector corpus from the exact-scan notebook. With `{python} AnnFootprint.links_str` eight-byte links per node, an HNSW graph adds `{python} AnnFootprint.graph_str` of edge topology to `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.footprint_str` of vectors. Because greedy routing traverses arbitrary graph links, memory access patterns are dominated by dependent random reads, requiring both the graph and the vectors to remain memory-resident. Product quantization with `{python} AnnFootprint.code_str` subvectors of `{python} AnnFootprint.sub_dim_str` dimensions stores `{python} AnnFootprint.codes_str` of codes, `{python} AnnFootprint.ratio_mult_str` smaller than the FP16 vectors, and its per-query lookup table occupies only `{python} AnnFootprint.lut_str`. @Tbl-vol3-ann-tradeoffs sets the three designs side by side.

| **Property**                  | **Exact scan**                                  | **IVF-PQ**                                                               | **HNSW**                                                                 |
|:------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Work per query**            | Every eligible vector                           | $\CoarseCellCount$ centroids plus the codes in $\ProbedCellCount$ cells  | Distances along a greedy path and a beam of width $\HnswSearchBeamWidth$ |
| **Resident bytes (notebook)** | `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.footprint_str` | `{python} AnnFootprint.codes_str` of codes, plus centroids and codebooks | `{python} AnnFootprint.total_hnsw_str` of vectors and links              |
| **Distance fidelity**         | Exact under the metric                          | Approximate; re-scoring a short list recovers it                         | Exact for each visited vector; misses come from unvisited ones           |
| **Recall knob**               | None needed                                     | $\ProbedCellCount$, $\PqSubvectorCount$                                  | $\HnswSearchBeamWidth$, $\HnswMaximumConnectionCount$                    |
| **Insert and delete**         | Append; delete by exclusion                     | Cheap append; centroids and codebooks age as the corpus drifts           | Insert runs a search and relinks neighbors; delete leaves a marked node  |
| **Memory access**             | Sequential streaming, bandwidth-bound           | Short sequential scans of small codes                                    | Dependent random reads, one per hop                                      |

: **Exact and approximate vector search**: Each design trades the bytes a query touches against recall and update cost. Footprints use the exact-scan notebook's hypothetical corpus and the stipulated index shapes above; measured latency and recall depend on the data, queries, and settings. {#tbl-vol3-ann-tradeoffs tbl-colwidths="[20,22,29,29]"}

Selecting among these index structures requires evaluating them against the specific record volumes, query distributions, and latency budgets the agent encounters. Systems engineers must also distinguish two evaluation metrics. Recall against an exact scan measures algorithmic fidelity to the mathematical distance metric, whereas end-to-end task success measures whether the retrieved records contain the requisite causal evidence to resolve the agent's objective.

The filtering hazard from lexical search (@sec-vol3-long-term-memory-search-scope) returns here in sharper form, because scope filters present greater friction on a graph index than on inverted postings lists. In lexical retrieval, intersecting a postings list with an eligibility bitset prunes unauthorized documents without altering how the remaining documents are traversed. In an HNSW graph, restricting search during traversal (pre-filtering) forces the beam to step exclusively onto eligible nodes. If a tenant boundary or file path mask isolates regions of the graph, the greedy walk stalls at a local minimum when all outgoing links lead to masked nodes. The search terminates prematurely and returns incomplete results, even when highly relevant eligible nodes exist just beyond the masked barrier. Conversely, filtering after an unconstrained search (post-filtering) risks returning an empty set whenever the top-$\RetrievalCutoffCount$ candidates fall outside the authorized scope. Systems escape the dilemma in one of three ways (@fig-vol3-access-prefilter). They partition the index into scope-isolated subgraphs, seed extra entry points inside the authorized region, or fall back to an exact scan when the filter is selective enough that the measured full request meets the budget, using the floor in notebook \ref{nbk-06-memory-bandwidth-and-latency-floor} as an initial feasibility screen.

::: {#fig-vol3-access-prefilter fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Filtering Inside a Graph Walk**: A scope mask applied during traversal (A) removes the only links between the entry region and the eligible vectors nearest $\SearchQueryEmbedding$, so the greedy walk stops at a local minimum and returns too few results even though eligible neighbors exist. The three responses (B) partition the index along scope boundaries, restart the walk from an entry point inside the eligible region, or, when the filter is selective, score every eligible vector exactly." fig-alt="Two panels. Panel A, mask applied during the walk, shows a graph split by a shaded vertical band labeled scope mask that contains dashed gray masked nodes. A blue arrow from an entry node reaches a green node circled in red and labeled stalls here; every link from the left eligible nodes to the right side passes through masked nodes, and the green nodes near a dashed query marker q on the right are labeled eligible near q, unreachable. Panel B, three responses, shows three rows: partition by scope, with separate graphs for scope X (green) and scope Y (gray dashed); extra entry point, where a blue entry node labeled extra entry starts the walk among green nodes near q; and exact scan when selective, with q and an arrow labeled score all pointing to a box of five green nodes."}
![](images/svg/retrieval_access_control_prefilter.svg)
:::

### Rank fusion and reranking {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-rank-fusion}

Production systems frequently combine multiple candidate-generation mechanisms through **hybrid retrieval**\index{Hybrid retrieval!definition}, pairing lexical keyword search with dense semantic retrieval. Before merging candidate lists, however, the runtime must establish unambiguous candidate identity based on tenant scope, source path, commit or version identifier, and span coordinates. Strict identity resolution ensures that an `r17` passage never erroneously merges with its modified `r18` counterpart, and that identical code in another tenant is never treated as authorized local evidence.

Because lexical scores (such as unbounded BM25 values) and dense similarity scores (such as cosine values in $[-1, 1]$) reside on non-comparable scales, directly normalizing or adding raw scores introduces calibration instability. **Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF)**\index{Reciprocal rank fusion!definition} bypasses score calibration by combining ranked lists based solely on candidate ordinal positions [@cormack2009reciprocal]. Let $\FusionInputList_i$ denote the list returned by method $\RetrievalMethodIndex$, and let $\FusionInputRank_i(\FusionCandidate)$ represent the 1-based rank of candidate $\FusionCandidate$ within that list. For a positive smoothing parameter $\RankFusionSmoothingConstant$, the truncated RRF score is defined as:

$$
\operatorname{RRF}(\FusionCandidate) = \sum_{i:\,\FusionCandidate\in \FusionInputList_i} \frac{1}{\RankFusionSmoothingConstant + \FusionInputRank_i(\FusionCandidate)}.
$$ {#eq-vol3-reciprocal-rank-fusion}

A candidate absent from a given list contributes zero from that source. Increasing $\RankFusionSmoothingConstant$ compresses the score differential between adjacent ranks without making the method entirely parameter-free;[^fn-rrf-rank-monotonicity] the runtime must also define an explicit tie-breaking convention and configure candidate cutoff depths for each retrieval path.

[^fn-rrf-rank-monotonicity]: **RRF score monotonicity**\index{Reciprocal rank fusion}: With fixed $\RankFusionSmoothingConstant > 0$, moving an item from rank $\FusionInputRank$ to $\PromotedFusionInputRank < \FusionInputRank$ in one input list increases its contribution by $1/(\RankFusionSmoothingConstant+\PromotedFusionInputRank)-1/(\RankFusionSmoothingConstant+\FusionInputRank)>0$ [@cormack2009reciprocal]. If its contributions from other lists do not decrease, its total score increases. This is a property of the item's score, not a guarantee of improved final rank when other candidates also change, or of relevant evidence.

```{python}
#| label: lego-06-reciprocal-rank-fusion
#| echo: false
# What: Reproduce an explicitly hypothetical pair of truncated candidate lists.
# How: Sum exact reciprocal ranks, then break score ties by stable candidate ID.
from fractions import Fraction
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_ratio

class HybridRankFusion:
    # LOAD: Assumed input ranks, not measurements of either retriever's quality.
    k = 60
    lexical = {"B": 1, "A": 2, "D": 3}
    dense = {"C": 1, "A": 2, "E": 3}

    # EXECUTE: Missing candidates contribute zero.
    scores = {}
    for ranking in (lexical, dense):
        for candidate, rank in ranking.items():
            scores[candidate] = scores.get(candidate, Fraction(0)) + Fraction(1, k + rank)
    ordered = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))
    fused_ranks = {}
    for rank, (candidate, score) in enumerate(ordered, start=1):
        fused_ranks[candidate] = rank

    # GUARD: Check agreement benefit and explicitly deterministic tied pairs.
    check(scores["A"] == Fraction(1, 31), "two second-place contributions")
    check(scores["B"] == scores["C"], "first-place tie")
    check(scores["D"] == scores["E"], "third-place tie")
    check(list(fused_ranks) == ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"], "stable tie order")

    # OUTPUT: Derived scores and final positions feed the table directly.
    k_str = fmt_int(k)
    a_score_str = fmt_ratio(float(scores["A"]), precision=5)
    b_score_str = fmt_ratio(float(scores["B"]), precision=5)
    c_score_str = fmt_ratio(float(scores["C"]), precision=5)
    d_score_str = fmt_ratio(float(scores["D"]), precision=5)
    e_score_str = fmt_ratio(float(scores["E"]), precision=5)
    a_rank_str = fmt_int(fused_ranks["A"])
    b_rank_str = fmt_int(fused_ranks["B"])
    c_rank_str = fmt_int(fused_ranks["C"])
    d_rank_str = fmt_int(fused_ranks["D"])
    e_rank_str = fmt_int(fused_ranks["E"])
```

To see how RRF rewards consensus across divergent retrieval mechanisms, consider an illustrative repair query evaluated on the authorized `r18` snapshot. Let A be the return-and-notify implementation span, B the reproducer test, and C, D, and E three additional candidate records. Suppose lexical search produces the ranking B, A, D, while dense retrieval produces C, A, E. With the standard choice $\RankFusionSmoothingConstant =$ `{python} HybridRankFusion.k_str`, @eq-vol3-reciprocal-rank-fusion assigns candidate A two second-place contributions, $1/(60+2) + 1/(60+2)$, whereas candidate B receives only a single first-place contribution of $1/(60+1)$. Summing every candidate's contributions in @tbl-vol3-rrf-scoring puts candidate A at the top fused rank on consensus across both retrieval paths, even though neither individual retriever ranked it first.

| Candidate | Lexical rank | Dense rank |                               RRF score |                         Fused position |
|:----------|-------------:|-----------:|----------------------------------------:|---------------------------------------:|
| A         |            2 |          2 | `{python} HybridRankFusion.a_score_str` | `{python} HybridRankFusion.a_rank_str` |
| B         |            1 |          — | `{python} HybridRankFusion.b_score_str` | `{python} HybridRankFusion.b_rank_str` |
| C         |            — |          1 | `{python} HybridRankFusion.c_score_str` | `{python} HybridRankFusion.c_rank_str` |
| D         |            3 |          — | `{python} HybridRankFusion.d_score_str` | `{python} HybridRankFusion.d_rank_str` |
| E         |            — |          3 | `{python} HybridRankFusion.e_score_str` | `{python} HybridRankFusion.e_rank_str` |

: **Fusion of hypothetical candidate rankings**: A benefits from appearing in both lists. A dash means absence from that truncated list and contributes zero. Equal scores are ordered by candidate ID, not by inferred relevance. {#tbl-vol3-rrf-scoring}

Dual consensus elevates candidate A for closer inspection, but agreement across two candidate generators remains an incomplete guarantee of relevance when both retrievers share systematic blind spots. To establish higher precision before staging evidence into the agent's context window, systems employ a **cross-encoder reranker**\index{Cross-encoder reranker!definition} [@nogueira2019passage]. Rather than scoring query and document independently, a cross-encoder runs the query and the candidate through the model together as one input, so every query token can attend to every candidate token. Because each score depends on a specific query and candidate pair, nothing can be computed before the query arrives, and this joint pass captures fine-grained token interactions at substantial query-time cost. A reranker can only reorder candidates already surfaced by upstream generators; it cannot retrieve missing records, and its score reflects structural and semantic resemblance rather than verified task applicability.

```{python}
#| label: lego-06-rerank-pool
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CROSS-ENCODER RERANKING WORK (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: reranking-cost paragraph in the rank-fusion subsection.
# │ Goal: Show that reranking work scales with pool size times pair length.
# │ Show: 50 candidates of 300 tokens with a 100-token query = 20,000 tokens.
# │ How: Stipulated token counts; no model or hardware latency claim.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int

class RerankPool:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Stipulated counts) ─────────────────────────────────────
    pool = 50
    passage_tokens = 300
    query_tokens = 100

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    pair_tokens = passage_tokens + query_tokens
    total = pool * pair_tokens

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(total == 20_000, "tokens processed per reranked query")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    pool_str = fmt_int(pool)
    passage_str = fmt_int(passage_tokens)
    query_str = fmt_int(query_tokens)
    total_str = fmt_int(total)
```

The substantial computational demand of this joint pass is why rerankers operate exclusively on short candidate pools. In a bi-encoder design, candidate vectors are computed offline, reducing query-time evaluation to a lightweight vector dot product. In a cross-encoder, query and candidate tokens must be processed jointly through the transformer layers, preventing offline precomputation. Computational cost scales with both candidate pool depth and token sequence length. For example, reranking a pool of `{python} RerankPool.pool_str` candidates of `{python} RerankPool.passage_str` tokens each against a `{python} RerankPool.query_str`-token query requires processing `{python} RerankPool.total_str` tokens, a prefill load comparable to a substantial model call, spent entirely on ordering. Systems manage this latency budget by constraining candidate pool sizes, invoking rerankers conditionally based on query ambiguity, or executing reranking asynchronously off the interactive path. The complete hybrid pipeline therefore narrows as it proceeds (@fig-vol3-hnsw-rrf). Two candidate generators feed a fusion step that needs only ranks, the costly reranker sees only the short fused pool, and the runtime stages a small labeled set within the payload budget.

::: {#fig-vol3-hnsw-rrf fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**From Candidate Lists to Staged Evidence**: Lexical and dense retrieval each rank candidates for the repair symptom. Candidates are joined on their full identity, so an r17 span never merges with its r18 counterpart, and reciprocal rank fusion combines ranks rather than raw scores, with the smoothing parameter $\RankFusionSmoothingConstant$ still a design choice. A cross-encoder reorders only a short pool, because its work grows with both pool size and pair length, and the runtime stages a small labeled set within the payload budget." fig-alt="Left-to-right pipeline. A query box labeled symptom branches to brackets beside two ranked lists: lexical (BM25) with B, A, D at ranks 1 to 3, and dense (ANN) with C, A, E at ranks 1 to 3, each list marked with its own shade of green. Both lists feed a box labeled join on identity (scope, path, version, span; r17 span differs from r18 span) and reciprocal rank fusion, which shows fused candidates A through E as horizontal bars built from one segment per list contribution, 1 over k rrf plus rank: A, outlined and labeled in bold green, has one lexical and one dense segment and is about twice as long as each single-segment bar for B, C, D, and E. A bracket labeled short pool around the top three fused candidates leads to a cross-encoder box, noted as work grows with pool and pair length, and then to a stage box holding two items labeled r18 within the payload budget."}
![](images/svg/vol3_ch06_hnsw_rrf.svg)
:::

Once reranked, top-ranked candidates pass into the staging pipeline (@sec-vol3-persistent-quarantine), where their provenance and authority are verified before injection into the agent's context payload. Even an optimally ranked evidence set, however, provides bounded guarantees. Retrieving the `r18` implementation and a passing reproducer confirms local syntax and isolated test execution, but it cannot prove that all concurrent caller paths remain race-free. Validating broader system properties requires corroborating records, such as runtime execution traces and multi-threaded test outcomes, that no single ranked list assembles on its own.

## Multi-Hop Retrieval {#sec-vol3-persistent-graphrag}

A single ranked passage often identifies an initial point of entry without delivering all the evidence an agent needs to make an informed engineering decision. In the connection-pool repair, the core implementation, the waiter-notification test, and the recorded test execution logs answer entirely distinct questions. Examining the pool implementation in isolation cannot reveal which execution paths the test actually exercised. Conversely, inspecting a passing test log leaves unanswered whether the change preserved wider public interface guarantees. **Multi-hop retrieval**\index{Multi-hop retrieval!definition} addresses this gap by traversing explicit relationships between evidence items, assembling an explanatory chain that no individual passage's retrieval score could justify alone.

Implementing multi-hop retrieval does not necessarily demand a dedicated graph database. An agent can inspect a retrieved passage, extract an unresolved reference, and issue a targeted tool call to fetch the next source artifact. Alternatively, an execution runtime can resolve known references ahead of time before invoking the model. Precomputing and maintaining explicit entity relationships pays off only when downstream queries reuse those links frequently enough to amortize the parsing and indexing overhead.

### Evidence paths {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-evidence-paths}

In diagnosing the connection pool bug, an effective evidence path originates at the recorded failure of `test_waiter_notified_on_return` under revision `r17`, explicitly scoped by its test revision and runtime environment. From there, the traversal traces from the test assertion in `tests/test_pool.py` directly into the pool operations exercised by the waiter-return scenario in `src/pool.py`. It then compares those source regions against the candidate patch in revision `r18` and its corresponding reproducer execution. Public interface contracts and unrelated callers remain isolated for subsequent targeted queries.

The edges along this path carry fundamentally distinct semantics. A link from a test run to a commit hash binds an outcome to an exact observed artifact; a static symbol reference in test code points to an implementation entity awaiting inspection; and a diff between revisions isolates textual code modifications. A robust retrieval payload preserves these labeled edge semantics alongside precise source locations and commit hashes. The runtime must also expose unresolved or broken links, such as a missing test log, an ambiguous dynamic dispatch target, or a traversal halted by a token budget. A static evidence path highlights plausible candidate root causes, but it cannot prove that those specific statements executed during the failing run, nor does it guarantee that all contributing dependencies were discovered.

### Maintained code graphs {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-code-graphs}

While a simple structural index records basic symbol definitions and usages, richer reasoning over software repositories demands structured relational models. A **code property graph**\index{Code property graph!definition} unifies abstract syntax trees, control-flow graphs, and program-dependence graphs into a single directed graph of program entities connected by typed edges [@yamaguchi2014modeling]. The edge types most relevant to software agents include syntactic containment and declaration, call edges connecting call sites to function targets, data-dependence edges tracking value definitions to their uses, type inheritance, and module-level imports.

Edge typing is what makes multi-hop graph traversal selective rather than combinatorial. In the connection-pool repair, restricting a search to invocation and mutation edges guides the traversal directly from `test_waiter_notified_on_return` to the pool's resource-return method, and onward to the waiter queue that the method mutates, skipping the dozens of unrelated files that merely import the pool module. The entry point for such a traversal, the seed node, can be resolved via an exact symbol lookup, an initial ranked passage retrieval, or an explicit file and line coordinate from an execution trace.

However, an edge is only as reliable as its underlying extraction mechanism. Lexical parsing reliably identifies declared syntax; resolving cross-file call targets requires complete type information and build configuration; dynamic execution traces observe only the concrete paths taken during a specific invocation. Systems graphs must therefore track provenance on every edge, ensuring the runtime never presents a statically inferred call as an observed runtime event. Furthermore, maintaining these graphs introduces ongoing invalidation overhead as the codebase evolves. A local edit to a method signature might invalidate caller graphs and dependent summaries across multiple repositories, whereas modifying an internal comment leaves structural edges unchanged. When source artifacts shift, any relationship whose underlying evidence has changed must be pruned or marked stale according to the update contracts established in @sec-vol3-persistent-invalidation.

### Bounded expansion {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-bounded-expansion}

Unconstrained expansion from a seed node quickly pulls in vastly more context than a downstream language model can process or attend to effectively. Traversal routines require strict operational guards: filtering permitted edge types, restricting traversal direction, capping maximum search depth, and bounding the total number of visited nodes. Tracking visited entity identifiers is essential to prevent cyclic loops from triggering infinite expansion. Even with structural bounds, context packing limits remain binding because a small handful of large code or documentation nodes can easily overrun the prompt budget.

Within these operational boundaries, the runtime can prioritize candidate nodes using semantic relevance, edge type affinities, or graph-centrality algorithms like Personalized PageRank [@page1999pagerank], which concentrates random-walk probability around the initial seed nodes. However, applying a naive score threshold across candidate nodes risks fragmenting the evidence chain. Preserving a coherent explanation often requires retaining an intermediate node with a lower individual query score simply to maintain topological connectivity between the seed and high-value leaf evidence, while compensating by pruning non-essential nodes elsewhere.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The personalized PageRank update and its unique fixed point are developed in @sec-vol3-appendix-math-pagerank.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_ltm_margin_depth_budget.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Four vertical bars for traversal depths 0 through 3, each taller than the last. A dashed horizontal line marks a 6,144-token allowance. The depth 2 bar, labeled 2,440, sits below the line in green; the depth 3 bar, labeled 7,300, rises above it in red."}

*One more level of depth turns a comfortable fit into an overflow.*
:::

Depth, more than node size, decides whether a neighborhood fits, and a tree simple enough to count exactly shows how sharply.

```{python}
#| label: lego-06-graph-neighborhood-expansion-vs-context
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: notebook nbk-06-graph-neighborhood-expansion-vs-context.
# │ Goal: Separate a traversal neighborhood from a serialized packing bound.
# │ Show: 40 reachable nodes require 7,300 tokens; at most 33 fit in 6,144.
# │ How: Count an exact tree, then apply a hypothetical final-serialization budget.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int

class GraphNeighborhoodExpansion:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario inputs) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    call_tokens = 32_768
    output_tokens = 2_048
    other_input_tokens = 24_576
    children = 3  # exact tree: every internal node has this many children
    depth = 3  # seed is depth zero; no repeated nodes
    node_tokens = 180  # fixed serialized size, including local provenance
    edge_envelope_tokens = 100  # stipulated total for either packing considered

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Integer token accounting) ─────────────────────────────────
    allowance = call_tokens - output_tokens - other_input_tokens
    nodes = (children ** (depth + 1) - 1) // (children - 1)
    required = nodes * node_tokens + edge_envelope_tokens
    fit = (allowance - edge_envelope_tokens) // node_tokens
    packed = fit * node_tokens + edge_envelope_tokens
    shallow_nodes = (children**depth - 1) // (children - 1)  # one level less
    shallow_required = shallow_nodes * node_tokens + edge_envelope_tokens

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(allowance == 6_144, "Match the chapter's retrieval allowance")
    check(nodes == 40 and required == 7_300, "Include seed and every level")
    check(fit == 33 and packed <= allowance, "Packing must fit")
    check(packed + node_tokens > allowance, "One more complete node cannot fit")
    check(required > allowance, "Full neighborhood exceeds the payload budget")
    check(shallow_nodes == 13 and shallow_required == 2_440 <= allowance, "One level shallower fits")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    children_str = fmt_int(children)
    depth_str = fmt_int(depth)
    nodes_str = fmt_int(nodes)
    node_tokens_str = fmt_int(node_tokens)
    edge_tokens_str = fmt_int(edge_envelope_tokens)
    allowance_str = fmt_int(allowance)
    required_str = fmt_int(required)
    fit_str = fmt_int(fit)
    shallow_depth_str = fmt_int(depth - 1)
    shallow_nodes_str = fmt_int(shallow_nodes)
    shallow_required_str = fmt_int(shallow_required)
```

::: {#nbk-06-graph-neighborhood-expansion-vs-context .callout-notebook title="Graph expansion and the evidence budget"}

**Problem**: Can the complete neighborhood around one seed fit the chapter's `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.allowance_str`-token retrieval allowance?

**Variables**: Suppose the neighborhood is a tree with exactly `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.children_str` children per internal node, explored through depth `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.depth_str`, with the seed at depth zero and no repeated nodes. Each complete node record occupies `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.node_tokens_str` serialized tokens, including its local provenance. Reserve `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.edge_tokens_str` tokens total for edge descriptions and the result envelope. All counts are hypothetical fixed serialization sizes.

**Math**: Counting the seed and all levels gives the geometric sum $1 + 3 + 9 + 27 = (3^{4}-1)/(3-1) =$ `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.nodes_str` nodes, in general $(\text{children}^{\text{depth}+1}-1)/(\text{children}-1)$. Staging them requires `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.nodes_str` $\times$ `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.node_tokens_str` $+$ `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.edge_tokens_str` $=$ `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.required_str` tokens, exceeding the allowance. With the same envelope reservation, the maximum number of complete equal-sized nodes is $\lfloor(6{,}144 - 100)/180\rfloor =$ `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.fit_str`.

Stopping one level earlier, at depth `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.shallow_depth_str`, stages all `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.shallow_nodes_str` nodes in `{python} GraphNeighborhoodExpansion.shallow_required_str` tokens.

**Systems insight**: Depth dominates traversal cost because every additional hop multiplies the expansion frontier by the graph's branching factor. A single extra level separates an evidence payload that comfortably fits the context window from one that overflows the allocation. Traversal engines must bound depth and filter edge types before ranking nodes; within those limits, scoring should prioritize nodes that preserve path connectivity rather than greedily selecting disconnected high-scoring fragments.

:::

Production code graphs exhibit clustered communities, cycles, and heavily skewed degree distributions. Consequently, calculating reachable nodes by raising an average branching factor to a traversal depth typically overestimates distinct reachable entities while underestimating the local search work required to evaluate candidate edges. When an evidence path exceeds the staging budget, the runtime must either narrow the query scope, return a truncated subgraph accompanied by an explicit continuation cursor, or defer downstream expansion to subsequent interactive agent turns. Under the absence rule, any traversal halted by an engineering limit must be explicitly reported as partial rather than exhausted.

### Community summaries as derived memory {#sec-vol3-graphrag-hierarchical}

Not every agent question resolves to a single evidence path. High-level architectural queries often span entire subsystems, for example how connection pooling, HTTP request dispatching, and transaction lifecycles interact across a service framework. Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) addresses these broader questions by constructing an entity knowledge graph and precomputing hierarchical summaries over densely connected subgraphs, or communities [@edge2024graphrag]. Unsupervised community detection[^fn-community-detection-graph] clusters related nodes based on network topology. However, whether a detected topological cluster corresponds to a true architectural boundary, and whether its generated natural-language summary remains technically accurate, are separate verification concerns.

[^fn-community-detection-graph]: **Community Detection**: GraphRAG partitions its entity graph using the Leiden algorithm, which refines modularity-based clustering to ensure that every detected community is well-separated and internally connected [@traag2019leiden]. Modularity optimization rewards groups with higher internal edge density than an equivalent random network. A detected community reflects entity co-occurrence density within the extracted corpora; whether that topological cluster corresponds to a logical module boundary recognized by system maintainers must be verified against actual source architecture. \index{Community detection!GraphRAG}

A derived summary amortizes token costs by synthesizing scattered facts into a concise artifact, but it remains a lossy, secondary representation. Every generated summary must retain bidirectional links to its source evidence, record the precise artifact revisions and operating parameters it describes, and inherit the most restrictive access label among its underlying inputs, so that a summary built partly from records restricted to one tenant is itself restricted to that tenant. Detailed execution plans should inspect the authoritative underlying records; the summary serves primarily as an indexed navigational map.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How labels propagate through summaries and other transformations under an information-flow policy is developed in @sec-vol3-security-label-propagation.
:::

For instance, an automated repair summary might record that revision `r18` passed `test_waiter_notified_on_return` under a specific thread-concurrency configuration. Because an observation is scoped to its tested configuration, this fact cannot be generalized into an assertion that "the connection pool is thread-safe." Moreover, precomputed summaries incur ongoing invalidation debt. Persisting an explicit dependency manifest between source files, detected communities, and generated summaries turns invalidation into a traversal of recorded dependencies rather than a guess. Any code modification flags all dependent summaries (and any higher-level rollups derived from them) as dirty. The runtime can continue to serve a dirty summary as a labeled historical snapshot until an offline job or on-demand trigger recompiles or invalidates it.

::: {#chk-06-hybrid-retrieval .callout-checkpoint title="Choosing and bounding related evidence"}

Apply these retrieval strategies to the running connection-pool repair.

- [ ] **Method choice**: A debugging query begins with an exact test identifier, but the subsequent inquiry requires identifying all upstream callers of the modified pool method. Which indexes or direct reads best support each step, and under what workload conditions does maintaining a persistent code property graph justify its synchronization overhead?
- [ ] **Evidence path**: Why does a static dependency path from a failing test to a pool implementation fail to prove the runtime root cause or guarantee the general correctness of patch `r18`?
- [ ] **Expansion estimate**: In the tree expansion model from notebook \ref{nbk-06-graph-neighborhood-expansion-vs-context}, if each node record shrank by half, how many levels could traversal proceed before exceeding the retrieval budget, and what computational search overhead would that additional level incur that serialization bounds fail to capture?
- [ ] **Derived summaries**: What provenance links and execution constraints must accompany a synthetic summary of a passing reproducer run to prevent a subsequent agent session from drawing invalid conclusions?

:::

Deciding whether to retain a detailed path explanation or a high-level subsystem summary is a write-policy decision, and that policy dictates the fidelity, staleness, and cost of the evidence that every subsequent agent session can retrieve.

## The Memory Write Path {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-write-path}

Retrieval can return only what the system has retained. An assistant that carries the directive “no meetings before 10:00” strictly within its current context window loses that constraint the moment the session terminates. Persisting the preference into long-term storage solves immediate conversational volatility, but it introduces the consistency challenge previewed in @sec-vol3-persistent-need. When the user later moves the boundary to 11:00, the runtime must ensure the earlier record stops governing new scheduling decisions without corrupting the historical audit trail.

The distinction between authoritative sources and derived records governs writes just as it governed reads (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}). A user's explicit directive provides direct evidence of an intent within a specific operational scope; an agent's internal paraphrase constitutes a lossy derived representation; and an automated rationale explaining why the user dislikes morning meetings is an ungrounded secondary inference. Storing all three artifacts as interchangeable assertions flattens evidentiary weight, depriving downstream retrieval pipelines of the ability to distinguish verified user intent from speculative model summaries.

::: {#dfn-06-memory-write-policy .callout-definition title="Memory write policy"}

A ***memory write policy***\index{Memory write policy!definition} is the runtime rule governing which proposed records enter durable storage, what claims and operational scopes they carry, and how the system subsequently corrects, supersedes, revalidates, expires, or deletes those records and their downstream derivations.

1.  **Significance**: Every admitted record becomes a candidate for retrieval in subsequent agent sessions. An unverified lesson admitted into storage can degrade the execution accuracy of every future task that retrieves it. The write path provides the most economical barrier against memory pollution because admission checks execute once per write rather than amortizing filtering costs across thousands of subsequent retrieval queries.
2.  **Distinction**: Storage retention simply preserves raw bytes in a database or index. The memory write policy governs the operational authority of those bytes, defining what claims an entry can justify and when it must stop influencing execution decisions.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Deduplicating writes based purely on embedding similarity, which erroneously discards near-identical updates (such as a revised meeting time or flipped boolean flag) as redundant duplicates.

:::

### Record scope and evidence {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-record-scope}

Every candidate memory record requires a concrete provenance tuple: an identifiable owner, an intended operational role, a bounded applicability scope, and verifiable backing evidence. For a scheduling preference, the scope must record the user identity, the target calendar, and explicit time zone constraints rather than leaving the runtime to guess ambient execution conditions. Furthermore, the runtime must enforce explicit consent boundaries: permission to inspect user messages during active reasoning does not grant permission to commit those details into durable storage.

Software repair trajectories generate a different class of evidence. For example, test execution records showing a failure at revision `r17` and a pass at revision `r18` represent immutable historical observations, but neither result justifies an unconditioned assertion about the codebase. A synthesized rule such as “inspect the return path when a waiter remains blocked” represents a heuristic hypothesis derived from that sequence, not a proven invariant. @Tbl-vol3-long-term-memory-write-policy formalizes these distinctions by categorizing how different memory records bind later execution.

| Record kind                          | Evidence retained                                                                  | Limit on later use                                                                    |
|:-------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Explicit preference                  | User statement, identity, scope, and statement version                             | Applies within that scope until revised or withdrawn                                  |
| Scoped observation                   | Tool result, checked revision, command, and relevant execution conditions          | Reports the observed case, not all later states                                       |
| Generated lesson or hypothesis       | Supporting observations, derivation, unresolved assumptions, and contrary evidence | Suggests an investigation; does not establish a new fact or grant authority           |
| Episode summary or continuation note | Task identifier and links to retained events and artifacts                         | Carries selected history or unfinished work; does not replace the underlying evidence |

: **Claims in agent-written memory**: Record kinds differ in what supports them and what a later task may infer from them. {#tbl-vol3-long-term-memory-write-policy}

These record kinds impose distinct demands across different operational archetypes. The research agent (lighthouse \ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}) and support agent (lighthouse \ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}) stress the memory write pipeline in different ways than the repair agent does.

::: {#lhs-06-memory-by-archetype .callout-lighthouse title="Persistent memory by archetype"}

@Tbl-vol3-memory-by-archetype sets the three workloads side by side, from the record each one keeps to the policy it leans on.

| **Lighthouse**     | **Dominant durable record**                             | **Source of record**                                   | **Binding hazard**                                              | **Write-policy emphasis**                                                     |
|:-------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Repair agent**   | Test observations and progress notes tied to revisions  | The repository at a source generation                  | Its own edits make indexed copies stale                         | Tag every observation with its revision; invalidate on the agent's own writes |
| **Research agent** | Notes and summaries distilled from fetched pages        | Each external page as fetched, with its time           | Untrusted text becomes a confident lesson through summarization | Admit distilled claims as hypotheses with links to the fetched pages          |
| **Support agent**  | Customer history, preferences, and answers about policy | The customer record and the published policy documents | A superseded preference or ungrounded policy answer is reused   | Supersede by explicit replacement; propagate deletion to every derived copy   |

: **Persistent memory by archetype**: The binding hazard, not the storage technology, decides which part of the write policy each workload stresses. {#tbl-vol3-memory-by-archetype tbl-colwidths="[14,22,20,22,22]"}

**Systems insight**: The repair agent's memory hazard comes from its own writes, the research agent's from other people's text, and the support agent's from time. One retrieval contract serves all three, and the write policy is where they diverge.

:::

### Admission before deduplication {#sec-vol3-memory-admission-gate}

An agent model may propose a memory write, but the runtime storage layer decides whether and how to persist it. Even when an architecture allows the language model to manage its active context by paging memory entries explicitly [@packer2023memgpt], context paging controls only working set occupancy; durable admission remains the exclusive responsibility of the storage runtime. The **admission gate**\index{Memory admission!definition} validates write permissions, confirms that the target store allows persistent retention for the active session, classifies the record type, and verifies that attached evidence satisfies the schema. Structural schema validation checks required fields such as timestamps and provenance identifiers.

Semantic fidelity, the requirement that the proposed record asserts nothing absent from the raw transcript, needs a check of its own, and that check is a verifier with error rates like any other. A deterministic check can validate a constrained structured input against the proposed record's owner, relation, value, and scope. Finding “11:00” in free-form text establishes only its occurrence; “11:00 applies only on Fridays” does not support an unrestricted scheduling preference. For free-text summaries, a calibrated model-based judge is one fallible fidelity check, and its false acceptance rate (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-check-precision) measures how often unsupported claims pass that check into durable storage, where every later session can retrieve them. Generating a summary and establishing that it is faithful are different events, which is the verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}) applied to memory admission. Sensitive data (such as credentials and private identifiers) demands strict classification and scrubbing policies; simple regular expression filters reliably fail on unstructured disclosures that match no standard secret pattern. When an agent proposes an interpretive conclusion lacking direct observational backing, the admission gate must either reject the candidate or downgrade it to an explicitly tagged hypothesis, preventing it from masquerading as a validated preference or concrete observation.

Only after passing admission validation does the runtime evaluate whether the candidate record inserts a new entry, updates an existing record, or duplicates existing knowledge. Vector similarity in an embedding space is useful for candidate retrieval, but it cannot resolve write semantics. If a user modifies a preference from “no meetings before 10:00” to “no meetings before 11:00,” the semantic embedding vectors are nearly identical. Relying on distance thresholds for deduplication would discard the update as an uninformative repeat, quietly dropping the user's explicit correction.

When an admitted record targets an existing entity under an identical scope, the runtime executes **supersession**\index{Supersession!definition}. The runtime creates a newly versioned record and marks the prior entry as superseded. This terminates the prior record's eligibility for active decision-making while preserving it in historical logs for auditing and provenance tracing. When scopes differ (for example, if the 11:00 restriction applies only to Fridays), both records remain valid within their respective domains. When scopes overlap ambiguously, the runtime must flag an unresolved conflict or prompt the user for clarification; heuristically synthesizing conflicting records into a fuzzy compromise produces brittle, ungrounded behavior. Furthermore, systems must distinguish an in-place correction from a true state transition. Fixing a transcription error that corrupted “10:00” repairs the fidelity of an existing record, whereas accepting an 11:00 update documents an authentic change in preference.

Concurrent updates demand explicit coordination primitives at the storage layer. A proposed supersession must carry the base version identifier against which it was generated. The store then evaluates and applies the update atomically through a compare-and-swap or conditional write, the same optimistic validation that context engineering applied to tool preconditions, closing the race inherent in separate read and write phases.\index{Optimistic concurrency control!memory writes} Optimistic validation suits memory writes particularly well. Two sessions seldom revise the same preference concurrently, so conflicts are rare, and a model call lasting several seconds makes a pessimistic lock impractical to hold across the invocation that proposes the write. When a collision does occur, the runtime must abort the write, reload the latest state, and re-evaluate the update against an explicit conflict resolution policy. Handing the conflict back to the model to blend the two states without transactional guarantees invites silent corruption.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Optimistic validation, which checks at commit that the state a decision read is unchanged and aborts otherwise, is established in @sec-vol3-context-engineering-change-detection.
:::

### Recorded observations and derived lessons {#sec-vol3-memory-dual-write-path}

Decoupling raw observational writes from downstream inductive derivation is essential for maintaining both prompt responsiveness and data integrity. When an agent executes an action, the runtime immediately writes the raw observation (the execution context, task ID, source revision, tool parameters, and raw output status) to durable storage. Only after this initial write does the runtime schedule background pipelines for summarization, embedding generation, and heuristic reflection. This separation guarantees that hard evidence persists even if downstream inference fails or crashes, while avoiding costly synchronous model calls on every execution step. Generating reflective summaries has demonstrated substantial empirical gains in autonomous error recovery [@shinn2023reflexion]; nonetheless, the resulting verbal reflections must enter the store strictly as generated hypotheses (@tbl-vol3-long-term-memory-write-policy), maintaining explicit foreign-key links to the raw observations from which they were induced.

Write acknowledgments must explicitly report the durability boundary achieved. Systems must distinguish among three distinct guarantees: *buffered in memory* (queued in an ephemeral local ring buffer), *committed to durable storage* (flushed to non-volatile disk or replicated across storage nodes under the durability contract), and *indexed for search* (visible to vector and keyword retrieval engines). Merely enqueuing an event into an in-memory worker queue provides zero crash durability. If a task requires strict persistence guarantees before taking non-reversible external actions, the runtime must block on storage confirmation rather than proceeding optimistically. Moreover, background indexing and reflection pipelines consume significant accelerator cycles and storage I/O; system schedulers must explicitly account for these background workloads to prevent asynchronous memory indexing from starving user-facing interactive inference.

### Revalidation, expiration, and deletion {#sec-vol3-memory-recency-decay}

A retained record changes status as its supporting evidence and operational context evolve. The superseded 10:00 preference and the `r17` test failure both remain valid historical records while losing eligibility for current decisions, and retaining historical snapshots remains a deliberate architectural policy choice.

**Revalidation**\index{Revalidation!definition} refreshes the empirical support for an existing record. For instance, asking the user to confirm that the 11:00 scheduling boundary remains active provides authoritative fresh evidence. In contrast, repeatedly retrieving an entry across dozens of successful runs indicates frequent utilization, not revalidation. Confusing usage frequency with validity is dangerous, because an unchecked error that is retrieved often is simply reused often, and each retrieval adds no evidence. Consequently, storage schemas must maintain distinct timestamps for record creation, last access, and last authoritative confirmation. Similarly, revalidating an automated diagnosis or heuristic rule derived from revision `r18` requires evaluating it against the current source code tree and active test environment, rather than treating age-based decay as a proxy for correctness.

**Expiration**\index{Memory expiration!definition} revokes a record's eligibility for decision-making once an expiration timestamp passes or a defined system condition is triggered. An expired temporary directive, such as an out-of-office scheduling window, must not govern subsequent actions without explicit reconfirmation. Some memory systems rank records by similarity multiplied by a recency factor that shrinks with age. Penalizing an expired record this way is inadequate, because if a query has few close semantic matches, an expired record with a penalized score can still surface in the top-$\RetrievalCutoffCount$ retrieval set and contaminate the prompt. Robust write paths enforce hard filtering, partitioning or tagging expired records so that operational retrieval filters exclude them unconditionally while retaining the payload for compliance auditing.

Deletion addresses the physical and logical lifecycle of the stored data. When a user revokes consent or asks to delete a preference, purging the primary database row is only the initial step. Stale representations frequently linger in secondary indexes, dense vector stores, consolidated episodic summaries, key-value caches, and pre-staged prompt templates managed by the runtime. The key-value case is easy to miss, because a cached prefix that contains the deleted preference still matches any request that repeats those tokens, and a prefix match certifies identical tokens, not current facts. The runtime must therefore evict that prefix or change the prompt so it no longer matches. A comprehensive deletion procedure must identify every downstream derivative, revoke its retrieval eligibility immediately, and schedule background reclamation or re-indexing under the governing data retention policy. To bridge the latency between request receipt and asynchronous garbage collection, systems write the storage counterpart of the marker that context invalidation places in a prompt. This **tombstone**\index{Tombstone!definition}[^fn-tombstone-death-certificate] is a durable exclusion record that filters the entity out of all active query paths before physical purging completes.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Why a prefix-cache hit verifies identical tokens rather than fresh evidence is established in @sec-vol3-kv-cache-prefix-compatibility.
:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Tombstones as masking records that log-structured storage engines keep until compaction, and their contrast with an advisory notice in a prompt, are established in @sec-vol3-context-engineering-invalidation-choice.
:::

[^fn-tombstone-death-certificate]: **Death Certificates**: Distributed replicated databases encountered this challenge decades ago. If a replica silently deletes an entry, a delayed update arriving from a partitioned peer appears to be fresh data and resurrects the deleted record. @demers1987epidemic resolved this in epidemic replication by writing an explicit “death certificate” that propagates through the cluster and supersedes older versions. In an agent memory architecture, lagging asynchronous indexers, pipeline queues, and restored snapshots function just like stale replicas, making durable tombstone markers necessary prior to physical deletion. \index{Tombstone!death certificate}

A deletion receipt must specify the exact boundary of guarantees achieved. Immutable cold backups, out-of-band external audit logs, and in-flight API payloads dispatched to third-party model providers lie outside the synchronous deletion perimeter. Deleting a record from runtime memory cannot retract a prompt token that an external foundation model has already processed, nor can it un-schedule a calendar invite already sent across an enterprise network. What the runtime can and must guarantee is that every internal index, cache, and prompt assembly buffer within its trust domain immediately ceases to use the deleted entity in future reasoning cycles.

### Consolidation {#sec-vol3-memory-consolidation}

**Consolidation**\index{Memory consolidation!definition} compresses clusters of related, fine-grained records into structured, high-level representations optimized for future retrieval. For instance, across a dozen debugging sessions on an asynchronous runtime, several granular test traces and failed stack frames can be consolidated into an architectural summary documenting which notification paths were evaluated, which revisions broke invariants, and which hypotheses remain open. Autonomous agent architectures frequently employ background workers to synthesize episodic observations into higher-level reflections [@park2023generative]. From a systems perspective, every consolidated reflection is a generated lesson (@tbl-vol3-long-term-memory-write-policy). Clustering records by embedding proximity helps identify candidate groups for consolidation, but vector similarity alone cannot establish causal relationships; verifying that two failures share an underlying defect requires structural evidence that semantic proximity cannot supply.

When generating consolidated records, the write pipeline must preserve provenance graphs, explicitly recording references to the constituent raw records, boundary conditions, and any observed counterexamples. Synthesizing multiple successful execution traces into an unconditioned, global procedure risks overgeneralizing domain-specific behavior. Furthermore, retaining the underlying source observations alongside the consolidated abstraction remains a deliberate architectural decision. Consolidated summaries minimize prompt tokens during inference, but stripping the raw logs removes the granular execution traces necessary for deep auditing and subsequent re-indexing.

### Self-reinforcing errors {#sec-vol3-memory-self-poisoning}

When an unverified hypothesis enters durable memory, subsequent summarization cycles risk treating the stored conjecture as an established premise, echoing and amplifying the error across successive generations of context. Under formal evidentiary rules, repeated retrieval and re-summarization provide zero independent validation. A faulty diagnostic guess that is copied into an episode summary, absorbed into a weekly milestone report, and ultimately consolidated into a cross-project heuristic still rests entirely on the original faulty inference. Memory poisoning\index{Memory poisoning} is the persistence of an unverified or withdrawn claim through the records derived from it. To prevent it, the storage engine must maintain rigorous dependency provenance across all derived artifacts. When an operator or verification pass invalidates a poisoned record, the invalidation must cascade through the entire dependency graph, retracting or marking as suspect every downstream summary and derived lesson. Merely down-ranking or tombstoning the root record is insufficient if derivative summaries continue circulating through retrieval indexes. Finally, even a fully validated, un-poisoned lesson functions merely as a candidate action suggestion; the execution engine must still enforce strict runtime authorization policies and environmental preconditions whenever an agent attempts to act on retrieved memories.

::: {#chk-06-memory-write-lifecycle .callout-checkpoint title="Following a preference through its lifecycle"}

A user changes “no meetings before 10:00” to “no meetings before 11:00” for the same calendar and later requests deletion of the preference. An index and a session summary still contain the original value.

- [ ] **Admission and revision**: Explain why semantic embedding similarity must not discard the 11:00 update, and identify the record that enters the superseded state.
- [ ] **Evidence and time**: The 11:00 preference was retrieved in 30 scheduling tasks across six months without explicit user revalidation. Should the runtime apply it to the next task without prompt confirmation, and which specific timestamp field determines this policy decision?
- [ ] **Withdrawal**: Enumerate all storage and cache representations that must stop influencing downstream prompts, and specify what guarantees the deletion acknowledgment can truthfully report if an immutable backup retains the raw record for 90 days.
- [ ] **Claim scope**: Contrast the evidentiary threshold required for an explicit user constraint against that required for an inductively generated scheduling heuristic.

:::

The memory write path establishes what a stored record claims, what evidence supports it, and when its operational validity ends. Those decisions reach the agent, however, only through derived indexes and caches that are rebuilt after the store changes, and until a lagging index catches up it can still answer with the record the write path just retired.

## Storage Invalidation {#sec-vol3-persistent-invalidation}

The connection-pool repair has reached revision `r18`, yet a subsequent search can still return an excerpt of `src/pool.py` indexed at `r17`. Consider how a single stale read unravels an otherwise systematic debugging trajectory:

1. At turn 12, the agent edits the return path in `src/pool.py`, and the workspace edit tool confirms the updated file at `r18`.
2. At turn 13, a search for the notification logic retrieves the `r17` chunk, which still contains the buggy line replaced in the previous turn, without a version label.
3. At turn 14, the model infers that its earlier modification was lost and reissues the edit. The edit tool rejects the request because the target snippet no longer exists in the current file.
4. At turn 15, the model confronts conflicting signals: a confirmed write, an excerpt contradicting that write, and a failed re-edit. It concludes that the workspace filesystem is corrupted and begins issuing speculative, wide-ranging edits. Each action burns context tokens and tool budget while driving the repository further from a reviewed state.

The unlabeled stale read initiates this failure by presenting an accurate historical excerpt as current state. The conflicting evidence does not establish filesystem corruption; a direct read of the current source could expose the mismatch. Model reasoning cannot reliably compensate for a retrieval layer that conceals which version its evidence describes. Each turn the trace wasted also lengthens the horizon over which per-turn errors compound (@eq-vol3-horizon-compounding).

Maintaining a persistent index forces a clean separation between two operations that an ephemeral staged prompt naturally couples: withholding obsolete records and generating their replacements.

::: {#dfn-06-storage-invalidation .callout-definition title="Storage invalidation"}

***Storage invalidation***\index{Storage invalidation!definition} is the exclusion of a derived record (an index entry, vector, summary, or cached result) from current-state retrieval once a relevant change to its source makes it inapplicable, independent of when a replacement is built.

1.  **Significance**: Coordinating exclusion with the source commit prevents known-obsolete entries from remaining eligible while their replacements are built. Notebook \ref{nbk-06-index-maintenance-cost} compares the additional metadata and indexing work, separately from the common durable commit and coordination costs. In the trace above, one unlabeled stale read cost three turns of the repair's budget.
2.  **Distinction**: Rebuilding synthesizes a replacement representation, whereas invalidation merely suppresses the obsolete one. This ensures that any query arriving during the rebuild window receives either an authoritative direct read or an explicit incomplete result rather than stale data.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Tracking staleness with an ephemeral dirty flag that clears automatically when a background job finishes. If an uncoordinated indexing worker completes late or a retrieval gateway restarts without durable tombstone state, obsolete entries can be erroneously readmitted.

:::

### Source generations {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-source-generations}

To guarantee freshness, an index entry must explicitly record the **source generation**\index{Source generation!definition} from which it was derived. A source generation is a monotonic version identity defined by the storage system's write contract, providing ordering guarantees that volatile filesystem modification timestamps cannot match. In the connection-pool repair, `r17` and `r18` denote successive repository states. Once the runtime establishes `r18` as the active generation, any query seeking current code must systematically discard entries tagged with `r17`.

Deciding which derived records an edit affects is the dependency tracking that context invalidation applied to staged observations, now applied to records that persist in the store and its indexes. What is new at this layer is that generations make the tracking durable across sessions, and that some derived records cannot be patched in place. Data dependencies often span beyond individual files.
