A raw code excerpt depends solely on its source file revision; a call-graph edge depends on multiple source files alongside the static-analysis configuration; an episodic summary depends on the tool outputs and diagnostic logs it consolidates. When an underlying artifact changes, the runtime must invalidate all affected downstream records while keeping unrelated entries intact. If the dependency graph is coarse or incomplete, the runtime must conservatively widen the invalidation boundary or explicitly report retrieval uncertainty. A missing dependency link must never be treated as proof of validity.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Tracking which claims depend on which observations, and propagating invalidation through that record, is established in @sec-vol3-context-engineering-claim-dependencies.
:::

From a systems standpoint, every retrieval index is a materialized view over base data, a problem relational database management systems have addressed for decades. Classical incremental view maintenance computes updates to a view algebraically from delta changes in base relations, bypassing the need to re-evaluate the full query [@blakeley1986efficiently; @gupta1995maintenance]. Unstructured retrieval indexes, however, resist algebraic delta maintenance. Under fixed-size chunking schemes, inserting even two lines near the beginning of a source file shifts the token boundaries of every subsequent chunk. Furthermore, deep neural embedding models are non-linear, so an updated vector cannot be synthesized from a vector subtraction and a text diff. Consequently, changed text requires discarding existing entries and running end-to-end forward passes to re-embed the new chunks. Practical retrieval architectures therefore decouple invalidation, a metadata exclusion coordinated with the source commit, from index rebuilding, which consumes substantial compute and network latency.

Beyond source generations, an embedding record must also encode the model identifier, tokenization pipeline, and preprocessing hyperparameters that generated it. A valid source generation confirms only that the underlying text is up to date; it does not indicate whether the vector remains compatible with the active retrieval model and query encoder.

### Source and index coordination {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-index-coordination}

Operationalizing this distinction requires a coordinated protocol among the storage coordinator, the indexing pipeline, and the retrieval gateway. This protocol assumes that the agent runtime governs workspace modifications, that the retrieval gateway can query an authoritative source generation along with its content, and that writes, index publications, and query admission share a coordination boundary, such as an atomic database transaction, a conditional write to a strongly consistent store whose replicas agree on a single commit order, or a local mutex. During an in-flight write, the gateway either holds queries within a tight latency deadline or marks the affected file scope as temporarily unavailable. A message queue or publish-subscribe broker alone cannot enforce these properties, because delivering a message is a separate event from committing the write it announces. A notice that `r18` committed can reach the gateway after a query has already been admitted against `r17`, and in that interval the gateway serves `r17` as current. The coordination sequence orchestrates a source modification while a straggling index worker remains active:

1. The source coordinator commits the patch as generation `r18` and atomically updates the active generation watermark for admission checks. Here a watermark is a position marker, the highest generation the gateway treats as current, not one of the compaction thresholds of context engineering. This prevents a visibility split where newly committed code is readable from disk while an out-of-band index registry continues to treat `r17` as current.
2. A subsequent query for `src/pool.py` retrieves candidate vectors derived from `r17` from the background index. The retrieval gateway checks their embedded generation tag against the active watermark (`r18`) and suppresses them. This exclusion signals index lag rather than a missing file or a failed edit.
3. An indexing job started prior to the commit finishes late. During index publication, the worker checks its captured generation within the coordination boundary. Recognizing that generation `r18` has superseded its input, the coordinator discards the stale output or redirects it to an archival store.
4. A fresh worker generates replacement vectors from an `r18` snapshot. It publishes them conditionally, committing the batch only if the workspace generation and index configuration remain unchanged throughout the indexing window.
5. Inbound queries continuously evaluate candidate generations against the active watermark. Publishing `r18` records never reactivates older `r17` entries, and background garbage collectors reclaim retired vectors on an independent schedule.

Publication validation and index installation must occur as a single atomic operation, because checking generation validity first and writing later introduces a time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition that allows concurrent edits to invalidate the payload. In-memory and durable tombstones record excluded generations while background workers rebuild representations. Because query admission enforces generation checks on every lookup, old candidates remain excluded even if temporary dirty flags clear prematurely. Similarly, deleting a source file installs a versioned tombstone, preventing delayed workers from accidentally resurrecting an obsolete record from an earlier snapshot.

Source generations allow the exclusion policy to be expressed in a compact, interval-based form. Each derived entry $\DerivedMemoryEntry$ carries a valid lifetime $[\MemoryEntryBirthGeneration(\DerivedMemoryEntry), \MemoryEntryDeathGeneration(\DerivedMemoryEntry))$, where $\MemoryEntryDeathGeneration(\DerivedMemoryEntry)$ remains open until a subsequent edit to that source scope closes the interval. A query evaluating workspace generation $\QueryWorkspaceGeneration$ admits candidate entry $\DerivedMemoryEntry$ if and only if

$$
\text{IsValid}(\DerivedMemoryEntry, \QueryWorkspaceGeneration) = \big(\MemoryEntryBirthGeneration(\DerivedMemoryEntry) \le \QueryWorkspaceGeneration < \MemoryEntryDeathGeneration(\DerivedMemoryEntry)\big).
$$ {#eq-vol3-index-validity}

For current-state execution, the runtime sets $\QueryWorkspaceGeneration$ to the active workspace generation. For historical diagnostics, such as an agent reviewing why an execution failed at revision `r17`, the query sets $\QueryWorkspaceGeneration$ to that historical revision. Subject to retention policies, @eq-vol3-index-validity serves both use cases uniformly, preventing historical data from masquerading as current state.

Exclusion solves freshness, but it introduces an efficiency trade-off that compounds over time. Suppressed records continue to occupy memory. In an HNSW graph, tombstoned nodes remain embedded in their neighbors' adjacency lists. Because greedy graph traversal continues to visit and evaluate these dead nodes before filtering them out at the admission boundary, a search with a fixed beam width explores fewer live items, degrading overall recall. To bound that loss, a background compaction process tracks the ratio of tombstoned records, $\TombstonedRecordFraction = \lvert \TombstonedNodeSet\rvert/\lvert \IndexGraphNodeSet\rvert$. When this ratio crosses a tuned threshold, the system builds a compacted graph: it purges unreferenced records, recomputes neighbor connections among surviving nodes, rebuilds navigation entry points, and atomically swaps the compacted index into memory. This workflow adopts the compaction design of log-structured merge-trees [@oneil1996log], balancing query latency and retrieval recall against the compute cost of background rebuilds. This is compaction in the storage-engine sense, rewriting a structure without its dead entries, not the summarization that context compaction performs on a prompt.

This coordination contract must remain robust against system restarts and uncoordinated writers. When a retrieval gateway restarts, it must reconstruct its authoritative generation state from durable storage before accepting queries; an empty in-memory tombstone table must never be treated as evidence that the index is fresh. Furthermore, if external tools or developers modify files without routing through the runtime coordinator, filesystem watcher events may arrive out of order or be dropped. In response, the gateway must fall back to direct, version-validated reads against the filesystem. If it cannot verify whether an indexed chunk matches disk before its query deadline expires, it must flag the result envelope as unverified rather than returning potentially stale data.

Replicated retrieval topologies require explicit **read-your-writes**\index{Read-your-writes consistency!definition}[^fn-session-guarantees-memory] guarantees, ensuring that an agent always observes the outcomes of its own preceding actions [@terry1994session]. When an agent issues a search following an edit, the query carries the log sequence number (LSN) corresponding to that write. A replica whose replay position (the last log entry it has applied) lags that LSN must pause execution within a bounded wait window. If the replica does not catch up before the deadline elapses, the gateway either routes the request to an authoritative primary or returns an explicit partial-status response.

[^fn-session-guarantees-memory]: **Session Guarantees**: The Bayou project established four foundational client-centric guarantees for weakly consistent distributed storage: read your writes, monotonic reads, writes follow reads, and monotonic writes [@terry1994session]. An agentic system requires more than simple read-your-writes behavior. For example, if an agent reads `r18` from an up-to-date replica and subsequently retrieves `r17` from a lagging node on the next step, the system violates monotonic reads, and the agent's view of workspace history moves backward. \index{Session guarantees!monotonic reads}

### Retrieval during index refresh {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-refresh-retrieval}

Excluding an obsolete candidate prevents an agent from consuming erroneous data, but it does not fulfill the retrieval layer's contract to return actionable context. When invalidation suppresses a record, the gateway must return an honest assessment of available evidence. As outlined in @tbl-vol3-invalidation-tradeoffs, a production retrieval layer can respond with one of three outcomes.

| Retrieval outcome             | Evidence supplied                                                                        | Remaining limitation                                                                                             |
|:------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Current indexed result        | Payload whose source generation and index configuration satisfy the request              | Ranking and bounded search can still omit relevant records; completion status must reflect the search performed. |
| Authorized direct source read | A bounded source excerpt with its observed version and provenance                        | Direct access can be expensive, unavailable, or too narrow to answer the whole query.                            |
| Explicit incomplete result    | Admissible partial evidence, or no payload, with an explanation of the unavailable scope | The caller lacks the requested evidence and must not infer that the source contains no match.                    |

: **Retrieval choices during index refresh**: Exclusion protects against known version mismatch; replacement retrieval and search completeness remain separate obligations. {#tbl-vol3-invalidation-tradeoffs tbl-colwidths="[24,36,40]"}

The appropriate fallback depends on query structure. For an explicit target path like `src/pool.py`, the gateway can execute an authorized direct source read, returning the live `r18` text while background embedding jobs run. Conversely, a broad semantic query, such as a search for all modules affected by a modified locking interface, cannot be answered by reading a single file. Answering it accurately requires either a refreshed semantic index or comprehensive static analysis across many files. If bounded direct reads cannot resolve the query within the execution budget, the gateway must return an explicit incomplete result. Artificially inflating candidate limits (such as expanding $\RetrievalCutoffCount$ during top-$\RetrievalCutoffCount$ nearest-neighbor retrieval) does not solve this problem: an unindexed record does not exist in the vector index, and no search depth can retrieve missing points.

Systems architects must decide where to place this maintenance overhead. Synchronous re-indexing moves parsing, chunking, and embedding directly onto the write path, guaranteeing that fresh representations exist before any subsequent tool executes. Background re-indexing acknowledges writes after the required durable source commit and coordinated exclusion, allowing tools to return before rebuilding finishes while relying on the gateway to manage queries during the refresh window. This architectural trade-off depends on workspace edit frequency and whether bounded direct reads can satisfy immediate downstream queries. As notebook \ref{nbk-06-index-maintenance-cost} quantifies, their additional indexing and local metadata work can differ by several orders of magnitude, and they also differ in what a query during the rebuild sees (@fig-vol3-index-invalidation). Synchronous re-indexing never exposes that interval but stalls the write, unchecked background indexing serves `r17` entries as current, and background indexing with exclusion suppresses `r17` and answers the query with a direct read or a partial result.

```{python}
#| label: lego-06-index-maintenance-cost
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ WHO PAYS FOR INDEX MAINTENANCE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-06-index-maintenance-cost
# │ Goal: Compare synchronous re-indexing on the write path with exclusion.
# │ Show: 88 ms local, 210 ms remote batched, 1.26 s remote per file; exclusion
# │       adds 0.4 us of local metadata updates and 1.5 us of lookups.
# │ How: Stipulated incremental work; common durable coordination excluded.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim.core.units import microsecond, millisecond, nanosecond, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_time

class IndexMaintenanceCost:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Stipulated edit and per-stage costs) ───────────────────
    files = 8
    chunks_per_file = 2
    t_parse = 3.5 * millisecond  # per file
    t_lex = 2.0 * millisecond  # per chunk
    t_embed_batch = 28.0 * millisecond  # one local batch
    batch = 16
    t_rpc = 150 * millisecond  # one remote embedding request
    t_excl_write = 50 * nanosecond  # local in-memory update per exclusion-table entry
    candidates = 50
    t_excl_check = 30 * nanosecond  # local in-memory lookup per candidate

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunks = files * chunks_per_file
    batches = math.ceil(chunks / batch)
    t_local = (files * t_parse + chunks * t_lex + batches * t_embed_batch).to(millisecond)
    t_remote = (files * t_parse + chunks * t_lex + batches * t_rpc).to(millisecond)
    t_serial = (files * t_parse + chunks * t_lex + files * t_rpc).to(second)
    t_write = (files * t_excl_write).to(microsecond)
    t_read = (candidates * t_excl_check).to(microsecond)
    write_path_ratio = (t_local / t_write).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(chunks == 16 and batches == 1, "one embedding batch")
    check(abs(t_local.magnitude - 88) < 1e-9, "local synchronous path")
    check(abs(t_remote.magnitude - 210) < 1e-9, "remote batched path")
    check(abs(t_serial.magnitude - 1.26) < 1e-9, "remote per-file path")
    check(t_local.to(microsecond) > 1e4 * t_write, "local metadata work is orders of magnitude cheaper")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    files_str = fmt_int(files)
    chunks_str = fmt_int(chunks)
    candidates_str = fmt_int(candidates)
    t_local_str = fmt_time(t_local, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_remote_str = fmt_time(t_remote, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_serial_str = fmt_time(t_serial, unit=second, precision=2)
    t_write_str = fmt_time(t_write, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    t_read_str = fmt_time(t_read, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    t_parse_str = fmt_time(t_parse, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_lex_str = fmt_time(t_lex, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_embed_batch_str = fmt_time(t_embed_batch, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    batch_str = fmt_int(batch)
    t_rpc_str = fmt_time(t_rpc, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_excl_write_str = fmt_time(t_excl_write, unit=nanosecond, precision=0)
    t_excl_check_str = fmt_time(t_excl_check, unit=nanosecond, precision=0)
    write_path_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(write_path_ratio, precision=0, commas=True)
```

::: {#nbk-06-index-maintenance-cost .callout-notebook title="Who pays for keeping the index current"}
**Problem**: The repair's next edit modifies `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.files_str` files across `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.chunks_str` indexed chunks. All strategies share the same durable source-commit and coordination boundary. The exclusion costs count only incremental in-memory metadata updates and lookups, excluding durable commit and replication, coordination contention, restart reconstruction, and fallback retrieval. Using stipulated per-stage costs (`{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_parse_str` to parse a file, `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_lex_str` to update one chunk's lexical postings, `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_embed_batch_str` for a local embedding batch of up to `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.batch_str` chunks, `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_rpc_str` for a remote embedding RPC, `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_excl_write_str` to record an exclusion entry, and `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_excl_check_str` to check an entry), how much additional indexing or local metadata work does each strategy add, and which path bears it?

**Math**: Synchronous re-indexing halts write completion until parsing, postings updates, and vector embeddings are fully finished. Backed by a local embedding model, this pipeline adds `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_local_str` directly to the write path. A single batched remote embedding call increases write overhead to `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_remote_str`, while serial remote requests per file inflate it to `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_serial_str`. In contrast, updating `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.files_str` local exclusion entries adds `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_write_str` of in-memory metadata work. Subsequent retrieval passes check `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.candidates_str` candidates against this metadata, adding `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_read_str` of local lookup work. The local re-indexing stages consume `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.write_path_ratio_mult_str` as much time as these metadata updates; this ratio does not compare complete durable write latencies.

**Systems insight**: Under the coordinated generation protocol, exclusion suppresses known-obsolete entries before subsequent admission, though it does not produce fresh representations immediately. The small local metadata costs do not price the complete durable enforcement path. The computational cost of re-indexing is not eliminated; it is deferred to background workers, requiring the query gateway to manage the staleness gap using the strategies in @tbl-vol3-invalidation-tradeoffs. Coordinate exclusion with the source commit. Consider synchronous re-indexing when dependent queries arrive before background pipelines can finish and bounded fallback cannot supply the required evidence.
:::

::: {#fig-vol3-index-invalidation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Three Responses to a Source Edit**: Synchronous re-indexing blocks the write until r18 entries exist, adding `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_local_str` to `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_serial_str` under the notebook's stipulated costs. Background re-indexing without a generation check returns after the source commit but admits r17 entries as current until the rebuild finishes. Background re-indexing with coordinated exclusion returns before rebuilding finishes; a query in the interval sees r17 excluded and receives a direct read or a partial result, and the worker publishes only if its generation is still current. The cost labels compare incremental indexing and local metadata work, excluding the common durable commit and coordination costs and any fallback retrieval. The time axis is schematic." fig-alt="Three stacked timelines on a shared time axis marked r18 committed and r18 entries ready, with the shaded refresh window between them; each timeline has rows for agent, worker, and index serves. Synchronous re-index, noted as incremental indexing work of 88 ms (local) to 1.26 s (remote, per file): after edit r18 the agent's write is blocked while the worker parses, updates postings, and embeds r18, the index serves r17 entries until r18 entries are ready, and a later query gets r18. Background re-index with no generation check, noted as rebuild off the write path: during the window a red query bar reads query gets r17 as current while the index row reads r17 admitted as current. Background re-index with exclusion, noted as local metadata work of 0.4 microseconds per write and 1.5 microseconds per query: during the window the index row reads r17 excluded, an amber query bar reads query: direct read or partial, and the worker row ends with publish if current."}
![](images/svg/episodic_wal_flow.svg)
:::

Retrieved evidence represents the source state observed at the moment of the read. In an agentic system, a concurrent write can land before the model finishes deliberating and invokes its chosen action. Any tool call whose correctness depends on an unmodified workspace must therefore enforce an execution-time precondition, such as an optimistic version check, at the tool boundary. The storage subsystem's core duty is to preserve and surface the exact generation metadata that this precondition requires.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The atomic conditional update that enforces this version precondition at the tool boundary is developed in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-conditional-updates.
:::

Source-generation checks suppress obsolete records, atomic publication prevents straggling workers from reinstating stale representations, and explicit fallback contracts clarify whether fresh evidence is available. Together, these mechanisms enforce internal storage consistency rather than task success. In accordance with the end-to-end argument [@saltzer1984endtoend], whether the `r18` patch truly resolves the stalled waiter can be established only at the system boundary through integration tests executed against the real runtime environment. What the storage layer guarantees to that boundary is an uncompromised, auditable record of the exact source generation reflected in every retrieved fact.

## Evaluating Memory Policies {#sec-vol3-persistent-governance-eval}

Excluding a stale failure trace from an earlier run keeps an outdated representation out of the agent's next request, but it does not ensure that the agent finds the fresh evidence needed to effect a repair. Conversely, a stored reflection might reproduce a recent passing test run accurately while overstating what the pass proves. Rigorous evaluation cannot treat memory as a static lookup table. It must follow information across its full lifecycle: from initial admission into persistent storage, through indexing, retrieval, and prompt staging, to the subsequent updates, supersessions, and deletions that maintain consistency as the environment evolves.

The appropriate unit of comparison is the *memory policy*. A memory policy encompasses what an agent writes, how it indexes and retrieves records, how it stages evidence in the prompt, and how it maintains that evidence across sessions. The retrieval index is merely one component of that policy. Component-level microbenchmarks help locate failures in search precision or index latency, but task-level outcomes ultimately decide whether the assembled policy satisfies operational acceptance criteria.

### Cross-session policy trials {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-policy-trials}

A controlled cross-session trial begins with a fixed source snapshot and an identical initial memory store. Evaluators provision each policy with an isolated environment, identical task sequences, and identical constraints on model inference, tool execution, and compute budgets. Records generated during one trial session may influence subsequent sessions within that same trial, since that cross-session behavior is what the trial measures, but they must never contaminate a parallel trial. Ground-truth reference answers, test fixtures, and evaluator annotations must remain strictly outside both writable and retrievable stores. If an agent can access evaluation artifacts, a policy can easily appear to learn when it is merely caching the answers to the test suite.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Evaluation leakage, including solutions that persistent memory carries from one run into the next, is developed in @sec-vol3-evaluation-gyms-leakage.
:::

The comparison in @tbl-vol3-memory-policy-comparison isolates the baseline benefit of raw persistence from the operational benefit of governing what persists. Across all experimental conditions, the system enforces identical access controls and action permissions. The "unchecked" condition isolates content admission alone, while all conditions experience external source modifications and user updates on the same synchronized fixture schedule.

| **Policy condition**                        | **Question the comparison tests**                                                                                             |
|:--------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| New memory writes disabled                  | Can the task be completed from the allowed sources without accumulating additional cross-session memory?                      |
| Unchecked memory writes                     | Does retaining proposed notes help later sessions, or propagate unsupported claims and duplicates?                            |
| Checked admission, no lifecycle maintenance | Do admission checks help initially but leave records misleading after later changes?                                          |
| Checked admission and lifecycle maintenance | Do correction, supersession, revalidation, expiry, and deletion preserve useful evidence under change, at an acceptable cost? |

: **Memory policy comparison**: Begin each condition from the same store and evaluate the same sequence of sessions. The conditions isolate responsibilities; none is an assumed empirical winner. {#tbl-vol3-memory-policy-comparison tbl-colwidths="[34,66]"}

The scheduling preference supplies a concrete lifecycle fixture: an initial preference recorded at 10:00, an explicit supersession at 11:00, and a user deletion request in a subsequent session. The evaluation tests whether the agent applies the active preference before deletion and complies with post-deletion invariants afterward. This requires inspecting every storage tier: primary vector and keyword indices, consolidated summaries, and staged prompt templates. An agent that suppresses the primary record from raw search results but still retrieves an unpruned summary containing the old preference violates its withdrawal contract. Furthermore, system backups or audit logs retained for regulatory compliance must fall under an explicit data-retention policy rather than being counted as active working memory.

Similarly, an iterative software-repair fixture retains the failing run at `r17`, records the subsequent passing run at `r18`, and then challenges a future agent session to distinguish historical debugging context from the current state of the implementation without inappropriately broadening the reproducer's scope. When source files change, the fixture tests two critical behaviors: a relevant source edit should trigger revalidation of dependent records, while an unrelated source edit tests whether the policy mistakenly discards valid, useful evidence.

Deterministic fixed-record probes isolate specific defects in admission filtering, retrieval ranking, or cache invalidation. Full task trials then allow policies to accumulate their own records across multi-turn interactions, causing their execution trajectories to diverge naturally over time. Evaluators must hold initial conditions and scoring rubrics constant across runs. When stochastic generation or environment variations introduce noise, evaluations must report the number of independent trials alongside the full distribution of outcomes rather than relying solely on mean performance.

### Retrieval relevance judgments {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-relevance-judgments}

Standard retrieval metrics depend on unambiguous relevance judgments. For each test query, the benchmark must define the eligible source snapshot, the authorized access scope, and the specific records relevant to the agent's immediate task. Relevance is temporal and context-dependent: the log of the failing run at `r17` may be relevant when an agent explains the history of a bug, but it is invalid evidence for whether the candidate at `r18` passes. Evaluation fixtures must explicitly label these distinctions rather than expecting an embedding model's similarity score to capture temporal validity.

Let $\RetrievedRecordSet_k$ be the set of distinct records returned up to cutoff $\RetrievalCutoffCount$, and let $\RelevantRecordSet$ be the set of labeled relevant records in the eligible snapshot. Precision at cutoff $\RetrievalCutoffCount$ is defined as

$$
\text{P}@\RetrievalCutoffCount = \frac{\lvert\RetrievedRecordSet_k \cap \RelevantRecordSet\rvert}{\RetrievalCutoffCount},
\qquad \RetrievalCutoffCount > 0.
$$ {#eq-vol3-precision-at-k}

The denominator is the target cutoff $\RetrievalCutoffCount$, not the number of records the retriever actually returned. Unfilled result positions receive zero credit. Under this formulation, an empty result set scores zero, ensuring that a policy that underfills its staged context cannot artificially outscore a policy that retrieves a broader set of useful evidence. In contrast, calculating precision strictly over the returned records (with $\lvert\RetrievedRecordSet_k\rvert$ in the denominator) can invert these rankings. Evaluators must explicitly declare their denominator convention and report the raw count of returned records alongside precision scores.

Recall measures the fraction of relevant evidence retrieved from the eligible store:

$$
\text{Recall}@\RetrievalCutoffCount = \frac{\lvert\RetrievedRecordSet_k \cap \RelevantRecordSet\rvert}{\lvert\RelevantRecordSet\rvert}.
$$ {#eq-vol3-recall-at-k}

When the relevant set $\RelevantRecordSet$ is empty, recall is mathematically undefined ($0/0$). Evaluators should isolate unanswerable queries into a dedicated reporting cohort, assessing whether the agent correctly recognizes the absence of supporting evidence or fabricates an unsupported claim. Keeping the completion status of every evaluation query visible ensures that such boundary conditions are not swept into an aggregate average.

When surfacing an immediate answer is paramount, Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) evaluates how quickly the system finds its first hit. MRR computes the arithmetic mean of the reciprocal rank of the first relevant record across all evaluated queries, scoring zero whenever no relevant item appears within cutoff $\RetrievalCutoffCount$. However, MRR is insensitive to whether the complete evidence required for a multi-hop reasoning chain was assembled. Multi-hop evaluation fixtures must separately verify that all required entity relationships and source versions are present.

Temporal applicability demands a separate metric. The **stale-return rate**\index{Stale-return rate!definition} is the fraction of current-state queries that return at least one record invalidated by subsequent source modifications. It measures the store one layer below the stale-support rate of context engineering (@eq-vol3-stale-support): stale-return counts what retrieval hands back, while stale-support counts decisions that rest on superseded evidence once it is in context, so a stale record that the runtime labels or excludes at staging raises the first without raising the second. Historical retrospective queries must be evaluated and reported separately. Because a retriever that returns nothing returns no stale records, a degenerate policy that returns zero results achieves a perfect stale-return rate of zero while completely failing the task. Consequently, stale-return rates must always be reported alongside recall and evidence coverage.

### Lifecycle outcomes and full costs {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-lifecycle-costs}

A comprehensive evaluation must account for the full operational lifecycle of memory updates. In supersession and deletion trials, evaluators track whether an updated or deleted record, along with all its downstream representations (index postings, graph edges, and cached summaries), reached the declared target state within an established deadline. The benchmark logs update latency, queue backlogs, and unresolved timeouts. In this analysis, expiring a record from active retrieval and physically purging it from persistent storage are distinct operations that require distinct accounting; describing a record loosely as "forgotten" obscures whether data was merely hidden from the read path or permanently deleted from the database.

End-to-end task acceptance remains the ultimate arbiter of system quality. The acceptance rate must be calculated across all admitted task trials, explicitly including timeouts, uncaught exceptions, and partial completions in the denominator. Satisfying an obsolete constraint is an operational failure, even if the retriever achieved high precision against a stale label set.

System resource accounting must respect the same strict evaluation boundaries. Cost accounting aggregates the end-to-end compute footprint: query generation, keyword search, dense similarity computation, cross-encoder reranking, model token usage, memory writes, offline consolidation, and background index compaction. This ledger must include asynchronous background operations that do not directly block foreground user requests, as well as deferred maintenance tasks lingering at the end of the evaluation window. Dividing the total expenditure by the number of successfully completed tasks yields the cost per accepted task (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task). If a system completes zero tasks, evaluators must report total expenditure and zero successes rather than computing an undefined or misleading ratio.

Storage measurements require equally clear accounting boundaries. Benchmarks should report raw source bytes separately from auxiliary structures, including inverted index postings, dense vector tables, graph adjacency lists, version metadata, and durability replicas. Authors must explicitly define whether their reported storage amplification represents auxiliary bytes divided by raw source bytes, or total stored bytes (source plus auxiliary) divided by raw source bytes. Similarly, update-latency benchmarks must compare equivalent operations: a full index rebuild against a full index rebuild, rather than comparing a complete re-indexing pass against an asynchronous tombstone lookup. Notebook \ref{nbk-06-storage-amplification} compares both metrics across two representative store architectures.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_ltm_margin_storage_ratio.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal bars of auxiliary bytes relative to the raw source. Store A, lexical plus graph, reaches 0.36 times; Store B, lexical plus dense, reaches 8.52 times, with the vector portion, about nine-tenths of the bar, highlighted."}

*Dense vectors multiply a store's auxiliary bytes by an order of magnitude.*
:::

```{python}
#| label: lego-06-storage-amplification
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STORAGE AMPLIFICATION AND RE-INDEX TIME (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-06-storage-amplification
# │ Goal: Show why lexical+graph and lexical+dense stores differ by an order
# │       of magnitude in auxiliary bytes and re-index time.
# │ Show: auxiliary ratio 0.36x vs 8.52x; re-index 34.1 ms vs 612 ms.
# │ How: Stipulated corpus, index shapes, and throughputs; HNSW shape reused
# │      from the ANN footprint cell.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_FP32, MB, byte, millisecond, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_multiple, fmt_time

class StorageAmplification:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Stipulated corpus, index shapes, throughputs) ──────────
    files = 50_000
    tokens_per_file = 200
    bytes_per_file = 800 * byte
    postings_per_token = 0.8 * byte
    edges_per_file = 4
    edge_bytes = 32 * byte
    passage_tokens = 100
    d = 768
    vec_width = BYTES_FP32
    links = AnnFootprint.links_per_node
    link_bytes = AnnFootprint.link_bytes
    edited = 15
    lex_rate = 1_250  # files per second
    parse_rate = 680  # files per second
    embed_rate = 50  # chunks per second

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    tokens = files * tokens_per_file
    raw = files * bytes_per_file
    postings = tokens * postings_per_token
    graph = files * edges_per_file * edge_bytes
    chunks = tokens // passage_tokens
    vectors = chunks * d * vec_width
    hnsw = chunks * links * link_bytes
    aux_a = postings + graph
    aux_b = postings + vectors + hnsw
    ratio_aux_a = (aux_a / raw).to("").magnitude
    ratio_aux_b = (aux_b / raw).to("").magnitude
    edited_chunks = edited * tokens_per_file // passage_tokens
    t_a = ((edited / lex_rate + edited / parse_rate) * second).to(millisecond)
    t_b = ((edited / lex_rate + edited_chunks / embed_rate) * second).to(millisecond)
    bytes_ratio = (aux_b / aux_a).to("").magnitude
    time_ratio = (t_b / t_a).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(chunks == 100_000 and edited_chunks == 30, "chunk counts")
    check(abs(ratio_aux_a - 0.36) < 1e-9 and abs(ratio_aux_b - 8.52) < 1e-9, "ratios")
    check(t_b > 10 * t_a, "dense re-index dominated by embedding")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    files_str = fmt_int(files)
    tokens_per_file_str = fmt_int(tokens_per_file)
    raw_str = fmt_memory(raw, unit=MB, precision=0)
    edges_str = fmt_int(edges_per_file)
    passage_str = fmt_int(passage_tokens)
    d_str = fmt_int(d)
    aux_a_str = fmt_memory(aux_a, unit=MB, precision=1)
    aux_b_str = fmt_memory(aux_b, unit=MB, precision=1)
    vectors_str = fmt_memory(vectors, unit=MB, precision=1)
    ratio_aux_a_mult_str = fmt_multiple(ratio_aux_a, precision=2)
    ratio_aux_b_mult_str = fmt_multiple(ratio_aux_b, precision=2)
    ratio_tot_a_mult_str = fmt_multiple(1 + ratio_aux_a, precision=2)
    ratio_tot_b_mult_str = fmt_multiple(1 + ratio_aux_b, precision=2)
    edited_str = fmt_int(edited)
    edited_chunks_str = fmt_int(edited_chunks)
    embed_rate_str = fmt_int(embed_rate)
    t_a_str = fmt_time(t_a, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_b_str = fmt_time(t_b, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    bytes_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(bytes_ratio), precision=0, approx=True)
    time_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(time_ratio), precision=0, approx=True)
```

::: {#nbk-06-storage-amplification .callout-notebook title="Why two memory stores differ by an order of magnitude"}
**Problem**: A hypothetical repository holds `{python} StorageAmplification.files_str` files of `{python} StorageAmplification.tokens_per_file_str` tokens each, `{python} StorageAmplification.raw_str` of source. Store A adds a BM25 index and a structural graph with `{python} StorageAmplification.edges_str` edges per file. Store B adds the same BM25 index plus `{python} StorageAmplification.passage_str`-token chunks embedded as `{python} StorageAmplification.d_str`-dimensional vectors under an HNSW graph shaped like the one in @tbl-vol3-ann-tradeoffs. The vectors are kept at full FP32 width, twice the FP16 width of the exact-scan corpus, and the encoder is stipulated to be slower than the local batch of notebook \ref{nbk-06-index-maintenance-cost}. How do their auxiliary bytes and re-index times compare?

**Math**: Store A's auxiliary structures occupy `{python} StorageAmplification.aux_a_str`, an auxiliary ratio of `{python} StorageAmplification.ratio_aux_a_mult_str` over the raw source (total ratio `{python} StorageAmplification.ratio_tot_a_mult_str`). Store B's occupy `{python} StorageAmplification.aux_b_str`, of which the vectors alone are `{python} StorageAmplification.vectors_str`, an auxiliary ratio of `{python} StorageAmplification.ratio_aux_b_mult_str` (total `{python} StorageAmplification.ratio_tot_b_mult_str`). After an edit to `{python} StorageAmplification.edited_str` files, at stipulated throughputs for postings updates and parsing, Store A re-indexes in `{python} StorageAmplification.t_a_str`. Store B must re-embed `{python} StorageAmplification.edited_chunks_str` chunks; at `{python} StorageAmplification.embed_rate_str` chunks per second it needs `{python} StorageAmplification.t_b_str`.

Store B carries `{python} StorageAmplification.bytes_ratio_mult_str` the auxiliary bytes of Store A and takes `{python} StorageAmplification.time_ratio_mult_str` as long to re-index.

**Systems insight**: Dense vectors dominate both the bytes and the maintenance time, because each chunk becomes hundreds of floating-point components produced by a model pass. Compressing the vectors attacks the byte term, and storing them at FP16 would halve the vector bytes; only a faster encoder or fewer re-embedded chunks attacks the time term, which sets the stale window after every edit. The time ratio therefore depends on the stipulated encoder throughput and shrinks with a faster encoder, while the byte ratio does not depend on it. A dense index is worth its order of magnitude only when it raises task acceptance enough to repay that maintenance in the cost per accepted task. The live-source baseline of @sec-vol3-long-term-memory-agentic-retrieval pays neither term, which is why it is the comparison every added index must beat.
:::

Staging depth warrants independent empirical measurement because task success does not increase monotonically with the retrieval cutoff $\RetrievalCutoffCount$. Recall@$\RetrievalCutoffCount$ (@eq-vol3-recall-at-k) cannot decrease as $\RetrievalCutoffCount$ increases, but every added record changes the prompt the model must use. Two effects that limit usable working context act together here. Each superficially similar but irrelevant passage adds to the softmax normalizer and so dilutes the attention the critical evidence receives (attention dilution), and a larger staged set pushes some of that evidence toward the middle of the prompt, where models use it least reliably (lost in the middle) [@liu2024lost]. Too few records starve the decision of evidence; too many bury it. The optimal operating range depends heavily on the model's attention architecture, task complexity, and reranker quality. This mirrors the working-set view of context (principle \ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set}). In practice, systems engineers should configure candidate retrieval to maximize recall, use a precise reranker to stage only a compact working set into the prompt, and systematically sweep staging depth across evaluation trials rather than assuming a single static cutoff.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Usable working context, with attention dilution and the lost-in-the-middle effect that bound it, is established in @sec-vol3-context-engineering-physics.
:::

Ultimately, memory evaluation yields a multidimensional trade-off space rather than a single scalar benchmark score. A more expansive memory store retains helpful edge-case experiences, but it also accumulates obsolete or contradictory records. Conversely, a strict admission gate shields the agent from spurious lessons at the expense of rejecting valuable domain context. Systems architects must systematically vary read and write policies under identical operational budgets, evaluating whether variations in accepted task outcomes stem from evidence coverage, temporal applicability, lifecycle maintenance failures, or compute and storage costs.

### Adversarial boundary tests {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-adversarial-tests}

A complete evaluation suite must subject the memory system to adversarial boundary tests. In an isolated evaluation sandbox, test harnesses inject synthetic credentials, probe unauthorized namespace boundaries, and retrieve documents embedded with indirect prompt injections [@greshake2023not]. The test suite evaluates two critical enforcement layers: whether the runtime intercepts and suppresses unauthorized reads and writes, and whether an adversarial payload survives in downstream consolidated summaries after the primary source document has been withdrawn.

Evaluators must capture both the model's proposed actions and the runtime's actual execution disposition. Logging both stages ensures that the evaluation distinguishes an attempted security breach from an executed vulnerability. The memory policy is accountable for the records it admits, indexes, and stages; the tool and runtime authorization subsystems are accountable for governing what the agent is permitted to execute against the external environment.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The general adversarial-evaluation method developed in @sec-vol3-security-evaluation specifies the trial and the attacker's capabilities and measures attack success beside useful completion.
:::

::: {#chk-vol3-memory-policy-evaluation .callout-checkpoint title="Evidence across sessions"}

A proposed memory policy raises retrieval scores on a static snapshot. Its authors have not tested updates, deletion, or later task outcomes.

- [ ] **Trial isolation**: How can an evaluation harness prevent one policy's stored reflections or reference answers from contaminating another policy's trial?
- [ ] **Update semantics**: Which later-session probes would distinguish successful preference supersession from keeping both conflicting preferences?
- [ ] **Withdrawal scope**: What must be inspected beyond the original record after a deletion request, and what retention limits must the result disclose?
- [ ] **Metric boundary**: Why can a zero stale-return rate coexist with failed retrieval, and which task and cost measurements would reveal the failure?
- [ ] **Cost per accepted task**: Policy B raises acceptance from 50 percent to 60 percent but adds background maintenance equal to a tenth of Policy A's attempt cost. Estimate whether its cost per accepted task rises or falls, and find the acceptance rate at which the two policies break even.

:::

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-fallacies}

Persistent memory systems fail when they grant a stored representation more operational authority than its underlying provenance supports, or when they treat write-time admission as a permanent guarantee of validity. The misconceptions below represent common architectural traps where design shortcuts produce silent state corruption, latency spikes, or degraded reasoning fidelity. Each item highlights an engineering trade-off whose quantitative systems cost is demonstrated in this chapter's accompanying notebooks.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *A near-duplicate memory carries no new information.*

The 10:00-to-11:00 revision at the admission gate (@sec-vol3-memory-admission-gate) is one instance of a wider class. A flipped flag ("notify me of failures" becoming "do not notify me of failures") and a scoped exception ("no meetings before 11:00 on Fridays") also land beside the record they modify in embedding space, yet the first reverses it and the second must coexist with it. A similarity threshold fails differently on each, dropping the reversal as a repeat and collapsing the exception into the general rule, so the agent either keeps the prohibited behavior or loses the narrower constraint. High geometric proximity does not imply semantic equivalence. An admission pipeline must first establish entity identity, scope, record kind, and explicit update semantics; geometric similarity should deduplicate storage only after verifying that the new record asserts no state change and no change of scope.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Treating a high-ranked record as current.*

Vector similarity scores indicate semantic or topical affinity with a query, but they convey nothing about temporal freshness, transactional validity, or operational authority. In the trace that opens @sec-vol3-persistent-invalidation, the outdated `r17` excerpt of `src/pool.py` ranks first for the notification query. At turn 13 the agent consumed it without a version label, concluded that its own completed edit had been lost, and spent the following turns re-issuing that edit and then making speculative changes that pushed the repository further from a reviewed state. Coordinated generation checks prevent this particular cascade. Filtering `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.candidates_str` candidates adds `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_read_str` of local metadata lookup work under the stipulated scenario, excluding the durable coordination and fallback costs (notebook \ref{nbk-06-index-maintenance-cost}). While index rank identifies candidate relevance, the runtime must rely on provenance, version tags, visibility scope, and completion status to govern how a retrieved record is applied.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *Staging more retrieved records gives the model more evidence.*

Recall@$\RetrievalCutoffCount$ cannot decrease as $\RetrievalCutoffCount$ grows, but task success does not follow it [@liu2024lost]. In notebook \ref{nbk-06-retrieval-payload-ledger}, a staging policy that counts only raw document bodies admits `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.body_only_str` records that serialize to `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.body_only_used_str` tokens, overrunning a `{python} RetrievalPayloadLedger.allowance_str`-token allowance before any of it reaches the model. Even within the allowance, the dilution and position effects that make staging depth a measured quantity rather than a maximum still apply. Systems architects must calibrate retrieval staging depth against downstream task completion and execution budgets rather than optimizing recall in isolation (@sec-vol3-persistent-governance-eval).
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Re-indexing synchronously on every write to keep the index current.*

Recomputing dense embeddings and rebuilding index graphs synchronously on every mutation introduces severe write latency and throughput bottlenecks. Under the stipulated costs of notebook \ref{nbk-06-index-maintenance-cost}, synchronous re-indexing adds between `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_local_str` and `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_serial_str` of blocking latency to every edit. Decoupling exclusion from rebuilding moves that work off the write path. The local exclusion updates take `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_write_str`, and each later query adds `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_read_str` of metadata lookups, excluding the common durable commit and coordination costs and any fallback retrieval. Replacement entries are built in the background. Blocking for fresh indexed representations can still be useful when dependent queries arrive inside the rebuild window and direct fallback cannot answer them within budget.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *Every dense store needs an approximate index, because an exact scan is too slow.*

Flat, exact vector scans scale linearly with the number of candidate vectors, but memory bandwidth alone carries substantial collections within tight latency budgets. In notebook \ref{nbk-06-memory-bandwidth-and-latency-floor}, an unindexed scan across `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.n_vectors_str` vectors has a streaming floor of `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.t_mem_str`. Applying a tenant or workspace filter beforehand reduces the candidate set to `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.n_filtered_str` vectors, dropping the streaming floor to `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.t_filtered_str`. A `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.t_budget_str` query budget gives an optimistic ceiling of `{python} VectorScanLatencyFloor.n_budget_str` vectors before query encoding, top-$\RetrievalCutoffCount$ selection, and record fetches are charged. Exact scans deliver perfect recall under the metric with zero graph construction overhead, no index fragmentation, and immediate write availability. The bandwidth floor rules out infeasible scans; measured full-request latency determines whether an exact scan meets the budget and whether an approximate index merits its maintenance overhead.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Evaluating memory on a static snapshot.*

Benchmarking a memory subsystem against a static snapshot conceals the operational costs and failure modes that emerge under continuous mutation. Snapshot benchmarks ignore index drift, synchronization lag, compaction overhead, and stale-read anomalies. In notebook \ref{nbk-06-storage-amplification}, modifying `{python} StorageAmplification.edited_str` files leaves a dense vector store without current entries for `{python} StorageAmplification.t_b_str`, compared to `{python} StorageAmplification.t_a_str` for a lexical and structural store, and every query in that window must fall back to a direct read or a partial result. Furthermore, static tests cannot uncover race conditions such as a delayed worker republishing superseded state or an explicitly deleted user preference persisting inside a rolled-up summary. Systems engineers must evaluate memory architectures using dynamic lifecycle fixtures (@sec-vol3-persistent-governance-eval), measuring end-to-end task completion, synchronization latency, and storage amplification across realistic write-read-delete workloads.
:::

## Summary {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-summary}
[]{#sec-vol3-ch6-summary}

A software repair agent needs far more than an index that matches text embeddings against a bug report. Reliable long-term memory requires the system to determine what each retained record represents, which authoritative source supports it, how context budgets constrain its entry into later requests, and how downstream state changes when that underlying support is modified. Retrieval methods locate candidates under an explicit operational contract; the write lifecycle governs which records survive to become candidates; and comprehensive evaluation ensures that engineers do not mistake improved search recall for genuine task performance.

@Tbl-vol3-long-term-memory-key-equations collects the quantitative relations governing long-term memory systems, linking each computational bound and operational threshold to the systems decision it informs.
