::: {.callout-takeaways title="Persistent information needs a lifecycle"}

* **Records retain different kinds of evidence**: Primary source records, agent observations, synthesized lessons, and retrieval indexes serve different roles in an evidence chain. Explicit provenance and scope allow downstream systems to distinguish an empirical execution outcome from a speculative hypothesis. System deployers remain strictly accountable when an aggregated summary or derived heuristic contradicts its underlying source of record.
* **A retrieval result has a contract**: Scope boundaries, access controls, version validity, payload budgets, and completion status dictate what enters prompt context. Formatting envelope overhead and metadata fields consume token allowances alongside record bodies, directly capping candidate capacity. An empty response from a partial or approximate search does not prove absence. Only a completed exhaustive search supports that conclusion within its declared scope and snapshot.
* **Search strategy follows the information need**: Key-value lookups, lexical ranking, dense vector similarity, and structural graph traversal address distinct retrieval requirements. An exact scan supplies the recall baseline under the chosen metric. Its bandwidth floor ($\EligibleVectorCount \EmbeddingDimension\ElementStorageSize/\Bandwidth$) rules out infeasible scans, while measured full-request latency determines whether it meets the search budget. Every auxiliary vector index or inverted list introduces ongoing write amplification and synchronization overhead, which pays off only when it delivers measurable gains in task accuracy.
* **Relationships need evidence and a budget**: Explicit graph edges connect scattered records into cohesive multi-hop evidence chains. Because candidate neighborhoods expand exponentially with traversal depth ($(\text{children}^{\text{depth}+1}-1)/(\text{children}-1)$), retrieval pipelines must enforce strict depth and branching limits before scoring nodes. Traversal paths indicate topological reachability rather than verified runtime execution traces, so the agent must treat discovered paths as structural hypotheses that require independent corroboration.
* **Memory must change as its support changes**: Updates, supersession, time-to-live expiration, and deletion policies dictate whether a record remains eligible for future prompts. Modifying or evicting a primary record invalidates all downstream summaries, embeddings, and inverted postings. Apparent near-duplicates frequently represent critical real-world state mutations rather than redundant text. Moreover, frequent read access indicates high utilization, but read volume alone does not validate the ongoing factual accuracy of stored state.
* **Exclusion and rebuilding incur different work**: In the stipulated scenario, local exclusion lookups take microseconds while replacement indexing takes milliseconds to seconds; durable coordination and fallback costs remain separate. Decoupling invalidation from background re-indexing through version-aware visibility windows ($\MemoryEntryBirthGeneration(\DerivedMemoryEntry) \le \QueryWorkspaceGeneration < \MemoryEntryDeathGeneration(\DerivedMemoryEntry)$) shields readers from stale state while asynchronous maintenance pipelines converge.
* **Evaluate memory policies across multi-session lifecycles**: Offline ranking benchmarks reveal candidate retrieval precision, but multi-session evaluations expose how agents compound diagnostic errors or accumulate stale context over time. System architects must assess competing memory architectures by their end-to-end task completion rate ($\AcceptanceProbability$), lifecycle contract compliance, and amortized cost per accepted task ($\CostPerAcceptedTask$), using isolated search metrics primarily to diagnose local failure modes.

:::

Authority always resides with the source of record (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}). Retrieval therefore operates as an enforceable contract governing scope, freshness, and context allowances, rather than an unconstrained similarity lookup, and locating a candidate record does not grant permission to inject it uncritically into downstream execution. The write lifecycle extends this discipline to all derived artifacts that agents generate across sessions, including summaries, graph entities, vector embeddings, and cached lessons. Every transformation must preserve the explicit provenance, boundary conditions, and uncertainty of the original evidence rather than silently amplifying tentative diagnostic guesses into durable facts.

## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-history}

Long before digital computers possessed the capacity to store vast text collections, researchers recognized that locating the right record among many is fundamentally a selection problem rather than a storage problem. In his influential vision of the memex, @bush1945memex imagined a desk-sized device that would house an individual's books, records, and correspondence, allowing the user to establish associative trails between related items. Bush observed that human memory operates by association rather than formal indexing, and he located the primary engineering difficulty in selection rather than physical storage capacity. Over the subsequent half-century, classical information retrieval transformed selection into mathematical measurement. @salton1975vector formalized documents and queries as term-weight vectors ranked by geometric similarity in a shared vector space. @sparckjones1972statistical supplied the statistical foundation of inverse document frequency, demonstrating that rare terms provide far higher discriminative power than common ones. Building on probabilistic relevance frameworks, the approximations formulated by @robertson1994simple culminated in BM25, which remains an exceptionally durable lexical ranking baseline across modern search engines. To make these rankings practical over large collections within tight latency budgets, systems designers turned to inverted files, postings lists optimized for compact compression and fast intersection [@zobel2006inverted]. Lexical matching, however, inevitably faced the vocabulary mismatch problem: users and authors routinely describe identical concepts using different words [@furnas1987vocabulary], an obstacle that ultimately required learned semantic representations.

A second lineage came from databases and distributed systems, which tackled the maintenance half of the problem long before retrieval systems confronted mutable state. Because an agent's retrieval index operates as a derived view over evolving execution logs and external environments, it inherits classical database maintenance obligations. Incremental view maintenance established the formal methods required to keep a derived table consistent with its mutating base relations without recomputing the entire view from scratch [@blakeley1986efficiently; @gupta1995maintenance]. To coordinate concurrent writes without restrictive locking, optimistic concurrency control conditioned updates on validation checks against read sets [@kung1981optimistic]. In distributed systems with weakly consistent replicas, epidemic replication algorithms proved that deletions must leave explicit tombstone markers; without them, lagging peers interpret the absence of a record as missing data and resurrect the deleted item [@demers1987epidemic]. Similarly, session guarantees formalized the exact consistency expectations, such as read-your-writes and monotonic reads, that clients require when querying lagging replicas [@terry1994session]. At the storage layer, the log-structured merge-tree turned append-only logging and deferred compaction of superseded entries into an essential systems pattern [@oneil1996log]. Each of these mechanisms directly reappears in modern agent memory architectures: a retrieval index is never merely a search structure, but a ranked materialized view over mutable history.

Learned retrieval joined these two lineages. Geometric relaxations such as locality-sensitive hashing initially emerged to help approximate nearest-neighbor search escape the curse of dimensionality [@indyk1998approximate]. Subsequently, product quantization [@jegou2011product] and navigable proximity graphs [@malkov2018efficient] made sub-linear vector search practical at the scale of billions of embeddings [@johnson2019billion]. In parallel, deep learning architectures began incorporating explicit memory components. Memory networks gave neural models a dedicated, addressable store to read and write outside their parameter weights [@weston2015memory]. Open-domain question answering then paired learned neural retrievers with reading comprehension models [@chen2017reading], and dense passage retrieval [@karpukhin2020dense] alongside retrieval-augmented generation [@lewis2020retrieval] made the retriever an end-to-end learned component of text generation. Agent architectures extended this paradigm by transforming the memory store into an active workspace that models write as well as read. Systems introduced interleaved search and reasoning traces [@yao2023react], operating-system-inspired virtual context paging [@packer2023memgpt], verbalized self-reflections to correct past failures [@shinn2023reflexion], and continuous observation streams consolidated periodically into higher-level reflections [@park2023generative]. What modern agent systems inherit from these combined lineages is the core engineering obligation developed throughout this chapter: an agent's memory record is dependable only to the extent that its provenance, version validity, and operational scope are explicitly guaranteed.

The following foundational works repay deeper study, organized in rough chronological progression:

- @bush1945memex frames personal knowledge management around associative trails and selective retrieval, demonstrating that the central challenge of agent memory, extracting relevant context from an expansive repository, predates digital computing.
- @robertson2009bm25 provides the authors' retrospective on the probabilistic relevance framework behind BM25, delivering an exceptionally clear explanation of why term saturation and document length normalization take their specific mathematical forms.
- @zobel2006inverted surveys inverted-file construction, postings compression, and fast top-$\RetrievalCutoffCount$ query evaluation, detailing the systems engineering that underlies every production lexical index.
- @terry1994session formalizes four client-centric session guarantees in a few compact pages. Read alongside @sec-vol3-persistent-invalidation, it clarifies precisely which guarantees a retrieval gateway must enforce when managing asynchronous memory updates.
- @jegou2011product and @malkov2018efficient establish the two dominant architectural patterns in modern vector indexing. The former details product quantization for aggressive vector compression and fast asymmetric distance computation, while the latter introduces Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs for sub-linear proximity routing. Both provide rigorous analyses of what each approximation sacrifices in recall vs. query latency.
- @park2023generative presents an end-to-end memory architecture for autonomous agents, combining continuous observation streams, multi-factor scoring (recency, importance, and relevance), and periodic hierarchical reflection. It serves as a concrete reference against which the record types and lifecycle contracts of this chapter can be evaluated.

## Exercises {#sec-vol3-long-term-memory-exercises}

Every quantity below is a hypothetical given chosen for round arithmetic, not a measurement of any system. Each problem ends in a decision; state the decision and the number that justifies it.

**1. Serializing a smaller call (Basic).** A call permits 16,384 tokens. The runtime reserves 1,024 for output, and all other serialized input occupies 11,264. The result envelope costs 96 tokens, and each retrieved record carries a 300-token body and 60 tokens of source, version, and provenance metadata.

(a) How many complete records fit, and how many tokens remain?
(b) A retrieval limit that counts only bodies would admit how many records, and by how much would their serialization overshoot the allowance?
(c) The task owner wants 13 records staged. Metadata cannot be dropped, because the version labels are what let the model tell `r17` from `r18`. What is the largest body excerpt per record that meets the request?
(d) Two more tool results adding 512 tokens of other input arrive before the call. How many complete records fit now, and which reservation should the runtime recompute before dispatch?

**2. Where the exact scan stops paying (Basic).** A tenant's store holds $\EligibleVectorCount = 2{,}000{,}000$ vectors of dimension $\EmbeddingDimension = 1{,}024$ in FP16 ($\ElementStorageSize = 2$ bytes). The host sustains 100 GB/s of memory bandwidth and 2 TFLOP/s of peak arithmetic, and each search has a 5 ms latency budget.

(a) Compute the bytes, FLOPs, and arithmetic intensity of one exact scan, and compare the intensity with the host's ridge point.
(b) What is the bandwidth floor for one full scan, and what optimistic eligible-vector ceiling does that floor set under the budget?
(c) A scope filter restricts most queries to one project of 150,000 vectors. Does the bandwidth floor rule out an exact scan, and what measurement would decide whether it meets the search budget?
(d) Would storing the full corpus as INT8 bring the bandwidth floor of an unfiltered exact scan within budget?

**3. How much agreement buys (Basic).** Lexical search returns P, Q, R, S in that order, and dense search returns S, T, P, U. Every candidate is fully scoped to the same `r18` snapshot, ties break by candidate identifier, and the runtime stages three records.

(a) With $\RankFusionSmoothingConstant = 60$, compute every fused score with @eq-vol3-reciprocal-rank-fusion and the staged set.
(b) Find the largest rank $\FusionInputRank$ at which a candidate appearing at rank $\FusionInputRank$ in both lists still outscores a candidate at rank 1 in only one list, for $\RankFusionSmoothingConstant = 60$ and for $\RankFusionSmoothingConstant = 1$.
(c) Candidate Q is the reproducer test the agent must read. Is there any positive $\RankFusionSmoothingConstant$ at which Q outranks P? How does Q reach the staged set at $\RankFusionSmoothingConstant = 60$, and what should the runtime do instead of relying on that?

**4. How much the task names (Intermediate).** Transfer the choice of retrieval policy (@sec-vol3-long-term-memory-agentic-retrieval) to the research agent (lighthouse \ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}), whose store holds notes distilled from fetched pages. Every model round takes 4 s, and retrieval operations are fast enough to ignore. Each note serializes to 600 tokens with its metadata, the retrieval allowance is 6,144 tokens, and everything retrieved stays in context until the answer. Three policies are available. A *direct read* stages exactly the records the task names, with no extra round. *Pre-staging* stages the top 8 ranked notes before the first call; when that set lacks needed evidence, the model falls back to probing for what is missing. A *model-directed probe* costs one model round and returns 2 notes. Every policy ends with one answer round. Three tasks arrive:

- R1: “Reconcile pinned notes `n-4412` and `n-4413`.” The evidence is those two notes. Pre-staging captures both with probability 0.9, and a miss costs one probe round. Directed search needs one probe round.
- R2: “What has earlier work in this project established about battery fade under fast charging?” The evidence is three unnamed notes. Pre-staging captures all three with probability 0.8, and a miss costs one probe round. Directed search needs two probe rounds.
- R3: “Trace where the 40 percent figure in `n-4412` came from.” The evidence is `n-4412` and three further notes, each found only from a citation in the one before. Pre-staging includes `n-4412` but captures the whole chain with probability 0.1, and a miss costs three dependent probe rounds. Directed search needs four dependent probe rounds.

(a) For R1, compute the expected latency and staged tokens of each policy. Which policy wins, and what does pre-staging add that the research agent's binding constraint makes costly?
(b) For R2, compare pre-staging with directed search in expected latency, expected staged tokens, and worst-case staged tokens against the allowance. Which should the runtime choose?
(c) For R3, compute the same quantities for pre-staging and for directed search. Why is pre-staging's lower expected latency not a reason to choose it?
(d) Design a policy for R3 that combines two of the three, and compute its latency and staged tokens. State the selection rule the three tasks illustrate, and name the property of a returned record that stays the same whichever policy retrieves it.

**5. Fitting an index in memory (Intermediate).** A research store holds $\EligibleVectorCount = 50{,}000{,}000$ passage vectors of dimension $\EmbeddingDimension = 768$ in FP16 on a host with 64 GB of memory available for the index. The candidate designs are an exact scan of the raw vectors, HNSW with 32 eight-byte links per vector, and IVF-PQ with $\PqSubvectorCount = 96$ one-byte subcodes, $\CoarseCellCount = 10{,}000$ FP16 coarse centroids, and an 8-byte record identifier per stored code.

(a) Which designs fit the memory budget? Compute the resident bytes of each.
(b) For IVF-PQ, give the subvector dimension, the per-query lookup-table size with FP32 entries, and the compression ratio over the FP16 vectors.
(c) With $\ProbedCellCount = 16$ and evenly filled cells, how many bytes of codes does one query scan, and how does that compare with the bytes read to compare the query against every coarse centroid? What does the comparison suggest about the next optimization?
(d) Full-precision re-scoring of a 100-candidate shortlist reads vectors from secondary storage. How many bytes does that fetch, what distance accuracy does it recover, and which upstream misses can it not repair?

**6. Synchronous re-indexing in a repair session (Intermediate).** Each edit in a repair session changes 5 files and 15 indexed chunks. Stipulated costs are 4 ms to parse a file, 2 ms to update one chunk's postings, 40 ms per local embedding batch of up to 8 chunks, 150 ms per batch on a remote service, 50 ns for a local in-memory exclusion update per file, and 30 ns for a local lookup on one of 40 candidates per query. All strategies share a durable source-commit and coordination boundary whose costs are excluded, along with fallback retrieval costs. Background rebuilding starts immediately after that commit and executes the stipulated stages serially without queueing. A session performs 60 edits, and the model's next dependent query arrives 2 s after each source commit.

(a) What write-path time does synchronous re-indexing add per edit with the local service, with the remote service, and over the whole session?
(b) What local metadata work does exclusion add per write and per query, and which costs are absent from this comparison?
(c) Under background re-indexing with exclusion, is any dependent query served while replacement entries are missing?
(d) A new runtime issues an automatic verification search 50 ms after every source commit. Which queries now fall inside the rebuild interval, what does the retrieval layer return for them, and does that change justify synchronous re-indexing?

**7. Deletion deadlines in a support store (Intermediate).** Transfer the invalidation analysis to the support agent (lighthouse \ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}). Its store holds 80,000,000 memory vectors under an HNSW graph, kept at constant size because inserts balance removals. Each day 2,000 customers request full deletion of their 40 records apiece, and 20,000 customers supersede one preference, tombstoning its old vector. Compaction is triggered at $\TombstonedRecordFraction = 0.10$, rebuilds the live graph at a stipulated 20,000 vectors per second, and each tombstone occupies 16 bytes of an in-memory exclusion set. Retention policy requires deleted content to be physically removed within 30 days.

(a) How many days until the $\TombstonedRecordFraction$ trigger fires, and what is $\TombstonedRecordFraction$ when the retention deadline arrives? Which constraint sets the compaction schedule?
(b) How long does one compaction take, and how large is the exclusion set just before it?
(c) Each superseded preference also appears in two session summaries of about 1,000 tokens each. How many summary tokens per day would regeneration cost, and what cheaper treatment does the write lifecycle allow for a summary that is only historical?
(d) The repair agent's binding hazard is its own edits making indexed copies stale. Name the support agent's binding hazard and the mechanism in this chapter that answers it.

**8. Typed edges as a budget control (Intermediate).** A structural graph around a seed function has, on average, 4 outgoing call edges and 10 import edges per node. The retrieval allowance is 8,192 tokens, each node record serializes to 200 tokens, and edges plus the envelope take 150 tokens. Treat the neighborhood as an exact tree with no repeated nodes.

(a) Through what depth does a traversal restricted to call edges fit, and through what depth does one that also follows imports fit?
(b) What is the largest number of complete nodes the allowance holds?
(c) Could trimming node records to 120 tokens let a depth-3 call-only traversal fit? What is the largest node record that would?
(d) Why would the exact-tree count overstate the staged size of a real repository graph, and why is that no reason to drop the depth bound?

**9. Does a dense index pay for itself? (Advanced).** Two memory policies serve the same repair workload with one attempt per task. Policy L, lexical plus structural retrieval, accepts 55 percent of tasks at \$0.80 per attempt. Policy D adds dense retrieval, accepts 62 percent, and stages more evidence, raising the attempt cost to \$0.84. It also re-embeds 20 chunks for each of 6 edits per task at \$0.0005 per chunk and carries \$0.01 per task of amortized vector storage. Its encoder processes 50 chunks per second.

(a) Compute $\CostPerAcceptedTask$ for both policies with @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task. Which is cheaper per accepted task?
(b) What acceptance rate must Policy D reach to break even with Policy L?
(c) How long does each edit leave the dense index without current entries, and what must the retrieval layer do for queries in that window?
(d) The vendor of Policy D's encoder reports that Recall@10 rose from 0.60 to 0.80 on a static snapshot. Critique the claim as evidence for adopting Policy D, and design the trial that would settle the decision.

**10. Redesigning a freshness scheme (Advanced).** A team proposes to keep a repair index current with a per-file dirty flag that is set when an edit commits and cleared when a rebuild finishes, plus a five-minute age limit measured from the worker's source capture. At expiry, an entry becomes ineligible immediately and is scheduled for re-indexing; until a replacement appears, the gateway returns an incomplete result. Every replica applies each primary update exactly 2 s after it commits there, and a publication replaces the file's current entries. Consider one timeline. At $\TimeInstant = -0.1$ s worker W1 captures `src/pool.py` at `r17` and begins indexing it. At $\TimeInstant = 0$ the agent commits `r18` and the flag is set. At $\TimeInstant = 0.5$ s worker W2 publishes `r18` entries and clears the flag. At $\TimeInstant = 0.7$ s W1 finishes and publishes its `r17` entries. No other publication occurs before W1's entries expire. The agent queries the file every 3 s from $\TimeInstant = 3$ s onward.

(a) Ignoring replicas, under the proposal, for how long are `r17` entries served as current, and how many of the agent's queries can receive them?
(b) Assign generation intervals to the `r17` and `r18` entries and apply @eq-vol3-index-validity with $\QueryWorkspaceGeneration$ = `r18`. Which entries are admitted, and what must W1's publication check do?
(c) A query issued at $\TimeInstant = 1$ s reaches a replica, carrying the log sequence number of the `r18` commit. Using the read-your-writes rule, compare a 0.5 s wait bound with a 1.5 s bound in added latency and in the evidence returned.
(d) Write the redesigned protocol as at most five rules, and state which part of the proposal, if any, survives.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From memory policy to tool execution"}

The memory policies in this chapter already assume controlled operations that read sources, search indexes, update records, and return bounded observations. A retrieved record names the version it observed, but whether the source still holds that version when an edit commits, and whether an update that timed out took effect at all, are questions no stored record can answer. Settling them requires an interface that separates a generated request from its authorization, execution, and reported outcome, the boundary Part III, Tool Use, develops. @Sec-vol3-tool-calling begins with the tool-call contract through which the repair's proposed reads and writes become permitted operations, so that retrieved information is never mistaken for permission to act.

:::

```{=latex}
\part{key:vol3_tools}
```
